title: Kimberly Guilfoyle Broke Trump’s Most Important Rule
excerpt: After half-heartedly including some actual professionals in his first administration, Donald Trump is now served almost exclusively by sycophants and family mem
body: After half-heartedly including some actual professionals in his first administration, Donald Trump is now served almost exclusively by sycophants and family members

The president has made clear that he cares about loyalty more than qualifications, but the astonishing incompetence and corruption of many of his appointees raises an obvious question: What does it take to get fired by Trump’s White House? Kimberly Guilfoyle’s resignation yesterday as ambassador to Greece provides some clues
Guilfoyle has been accused of blatant corruption both before and during her time as an envoy
She denies these allegations, but her resignation—which the White House requested—isn’t really about corruption
The idea that Guilfoyle, and only Guilfoyle, crossed some sort of previously unseen corruption red line is laughable

If ethical and legal questions, including the now-moribund standard of “appearances of impropriety,” were grounds for dismissal in this administration, Trump would have already shed several other members of his team
Rather, Guilfoyle was pushed out because she was an embarrassment
She overstepped her bounds, tried to trade on the president’s name, and then made the administration look bad when she got caught
Also, she is a woman, and in this administration, self-dealing is mostly a man’s game
Indeed, by comparison with the charges leveled at others—including against the president himself, who seems utterly unconcerned with notions such as “emoluments”—Guilfoyle is decidedly a small-timer

This past spring, for example, the Financial Times reported that a broker for Pete Hegseth attempted to make a big investment in defense industries just before the Iran war, raising suspicions of insider trading

FBI Director Kash Patel has been accused of using government money as a slush fund to pay improper bonuses to his favorites within the Bureau. “Border Czar” Tom Homan was caught on audio in 2024 accepting $50,000 in cash (wrapped in a Cava food bag , always the sign of a deal on the up-and-up) from undercover FBI agents posing as business executives, and yet he remains in his job
Hegseth and Homan deny any wrongdoing; Patel and the FBI have offered no comment or explanation

And the journalist Dexter Filkins recently described Trump’s son-in-law and roving minister-without-portfolio Jared Kushner as representative of “a new kind of Washington figure, for whom public office serves as a means to extraordinary wealth.” [ Read: Trump’s team of mercenaries ] Guilfoyle may have been a relative piker among giants in the grift game, but her real sin was the pathetic and humiliating nature of her behavior. (Even Homan managed not to seem quite so grubby when reportedly accepting a bag of greenbacks.) Her messages to a Trump donor asking for money to help pay her huge credit-card bills are cringe-inducing. “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote to the Trump supporter Eric Deters when asking him to wire a cool $100,000 directly into her American Express account in July 2025, just before her confirmation hearings
Worse, she continually told Deters to stop writing things down and just contact her on Signal. “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” she said

This was apparently Guilfoyle’s version of the infamous “Stringer Bell rule,” named for a character from the television series The Wire who dressed down one of his drug-dealing accomplices for being stupid enough to keep written notes on a criminal conspiracy
The problem is that she, too, violated that rule: She made her requests to Deters to stop writing things down in writing
Deters, unsurprisingly, kept all the messages
Guilfoyle, he asserts, offered him access to the Trump administration. “I will be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever,” he claims she told him
When she didn’t deliver, he warned Guilfoyle and White House officials earlier this month that he would go public with their correspondence and then made good on that threat
The newly minted ambassador, meanwhile, was flitting about southeastern Europe in the company of Greek tycoons

But again, rather than enjoy the perks of her job in discreet luxury, she bragged about her connections to these wealthy men and tried to present herself as some sort of made woman from the inner Trump orbit who had the juice to get things done
According to The Wall Street Journal , she went to Davos in January 2026 and was excluded from a dinner being held for Eric Trump
She decided to pressure an American businessman to help her get in. “You know, I can deliver the world to you
Which you deserve,” she said. (This time, she was caught on audio , rather than by text message.) “I’m going to make you a lot of fucking money,” she told the American
She also raged about the impudence of the dinner’s Greek hostess. “You don’t have the fucking U.S., you know, ambassador to Greece not come
She should be kissing my fucking ass.” Again, Trump Sr. has no problem with F-bombs; he deploys them regularly

He has no problem with money grabs while in public office; he has enriched himself while president and has explicitly or implicitly blessed similar efforts by other subordinates to profit from their positions

But he apparently draws a line when his son’s former fiancée does not show proper appreciation for the courtesy of being stashed in Athens— Athens!— and then lands in the newspapers looking like an aging waitress cadging tips from marks in a casino

Don’t tell my manager, and I’ll get you to the good poker table. [ David Frum: Trump’s last loyal constituency ] Guilfoyle was once so tight with the Trumps that she was given a prime-time slot to fawn over the president during the 2020 GOP convention
It was a disastrous, over-the-top performance, but Trump loved it, reportedly calling her “my Kimberly” and comparing her to the former Argentine first lady Eva Perón
Earlier this year, Trump said of his emissary to Greece: “Kimberly Guilfoyle has been my friend for a long time

That’s my little pet name, right? But you are the greatest, and I heard they love you over there.” But over the past several days, the president saw bad publicity about this demanding, middle-aged woman, thrown over by his son for a younger wife—as Trump himself has done to previous spouses—trying to profit off his presidency while making a fool of herself and encouraging more bad press about corruption just before the midterm elections

Guilfoyle had to go, and Trump jettisoned her quickly and coldly. “She wasn’t a member of my family,” the president said yesterday. “She, uh, I guess dated my son a long time ago.” “Dated”? I guess ? She was in line for years to become the president’s daughter-in-law, married to his first-born son
Now she’s just some dame one of his kids used to know
All she had to do was stay out of trouble
But that was too hard for her, and now she’s learned that making money off this presidency means following some rules
Don’t be too obvious; don’t embarrass the boss; don’t get caught if you can help it
And especially, don’t be an older woman .

title: How Trump Is Selling Out Ukraine
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum discusses President Trump’s announced die
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum discusses President Trump’s announced diesel deal with Russia, the administration’s abandonment of Ukraine, and why Trump is giving up so much to gain very little
Then, David is joined from Kyiv by Illia Ponomarenko, a Ukrainian journalist and the author of the new book The Land of Tears and Hope
David and Illia talk about the history of Ukraine, its current state as the war with Russia rages on, and how and why the Trump administration seems so hostile to the country
Finally, David concludes with discussion about why so little literature exists about the history of slavery in Eastern Europe

The following is a transcript of the episode: David Frum: Those Americans who want the United States to take a more pro-Russian point of view or who denigrate the Ukrainian cause—the vice president of the United States and the people around him—they will insist that this war is about NATO expansion
But when you actually listen to actual Russians, they say, No, no, no; this is all about Yaroslav the Wise
And from a Russian point of view, this is not about NATO expansion, except when they’re talking in English to gullible Americans. [ Music ] David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic
My guest this week will be Illia Ponomarenko, author of a new history of Ukraine, Land of Tears and Hope, available from Bloomsbury in the month of November

Illia and I will discuss the deep history of Ukraine, the recent onslaught of Russian drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities, and how Ukrainians feel about their abandonment by the Trump administration
This week’s book will also be Eastern European–focused

It’s a book that I would like to read, and I set out a research assignment for some intrepid Eastern Europeanist to deliver a book I would like to know more about in, again, in the deep history of the lands that are now Ukraine, now Poland, and now Russia
But before either the dialogue with Illia or the book discussion, some opening thoughts about the most shocking recent turn in the U.S.-Ukraine story

When Illia and I recorded our dialogue, we did not yet know about this announcement that was pending from the Trump administration, declaring or imagining or proposing, or whatever the word is, for what is likely vaporware
Not a real deal; a big purchase, a massive—in the words of President Trump—a massive purchase of Russian diesel fuel for the United States
Now, I wrote an article for The Atlantic this past weekend with the facts and figures about just how negligible an achievement this so-called deal really is
It’s probably the largest producer of diesel on Earth
We don’t exactly know that for sure, because we don’t know really how much China produces, but probably the United States is the largest producer of diesel in the world
It is certainly the largest exporter of diesel in the world
And it produces much more than it uses at home
So it exports about a million and a half barrels of diesel fuel a day

The reason American prices have been rising so fast for truckers and farmers and others who use diesel fuel is not because of anything that’s happening in the U.S. market, or even the North American market

The United States imports a little diesel fuel from Canada because it’s easier sometimes to import from Canada and then to export from the Gulf Coast than to supply the United States entirely from its own resources
The reason that the price has been rising is because of disturbances in the global market
What matters is world demand and world supply of diesel, not U.S. demand and U.S. supply of diesel
Now, if this Russian deal exists at all, it’s a matter of a few hours’ worth of U.S. production and U.S. consumption
It’s not a big event, and it won’t change world prices because Russia doesn’t have a lot of diesel to sell
Although Russia used to be a big diesel producer, Russian oil facilities have been damaged so intensely by Ukrainian missile and drone fire that Russia has very little diesel to contribute
In fact, Russia has had an export ban on diesel since July
If Russia has any diesel to sell, it’s going to take it from another consumer; India, maybe
And by diverting diesel oil from India to the United States, it doesn’t do anything for the United States, which has more than enough diesel here at home
It makes life a little tougher for India, and it doesn’t change the world price at all, because nothing happens in global supply and demand
The whole thing is a complete nothingburger
But it does two things that are important
The first is: The Russians have dangled in front of the Trump inner circle the prospect of enormous wealth for them if American sanctions on Russia are dismantled

And it’s taken a first step toward the dismantling of those sanctions and put the United States on the path to confrontation with Ukraine, because President Trump now has to worry the only way he can get Russian diesel is if the Ukrainians stop attacking Russian energy facilities, which they are doing in retaliation for the Russian attacks on their cities and schools and historical societies and hospitals, on their civilian population
They have struck back against Russian energy infrastructure to cramp Russia’s war-making ability

President Trump has now created a situation where his goal of seeming to do something about diesel and maybe also enriching a lot of people who are in his inner circle is in conflict with Ukraine’s self-defense, and the only way he can get what he wants is by ordering Ukraine to stop defending itself
And we have seen already Trump’s pressure on Ukraine: If you continue to strike the Russian energy infrastructure, you are making an enemy of me
He is taking away Ukraine’s war-making ability for his own reasons, in ways that will not help American motorists even slightly, American farmers, American truckers

title: The Rise of In-Office Remote Work
excerpt: Home Depot, Instagram, Fidelity, and TikTok are just a few of the companies that have recently ordered their employees back to the office five days a week, part
body: Home Depot, Instagram, Fidelity, and TikTok are just a few of the companies that have recently ordered their employees back to the office five days a week, part of a broader shift toward stricter return-to-office mandates
Such policies cut down on working from home, yet they don’t always cut down on remote work
Many employees now commute to the office only to spend each day on video calls with colleagues who are elsewhere, or even down the hall
They’re in the office but still working remotely
We are two economists who have spent years studying how remote work shapes learning, productivity, happiness, and career progression
We have been struck by how often people picture the alternative to working from home as an office where nearly everyone is together
The modern office looks very different from that ideal
Today, the alternative to working from home is often working in a sea of mostly empty cubicles

In a September survey of 1,835 college-educated American workers, we found that, on their most recent day at the office, more than 70 percent of respondents had at least one member of their team who was not in the building with them
As a result, roughly half of respondents had no fully in-person meetings
And more than a third had exclusively online meetings because their teams moved meetings entirely online whenever anyone was remote
For these workers, the commute to the office buys little more than a different background on their video calls
The typical American spends 54 minutes getting to and from work in a day, which they rank among their most hated activities
Yet when colleagues are actually together, this commute can be worth it. [ Stephanie H
Murray: “Commuting is bad”—particularly for women ] In-person connection often unlocks the best parts of work
It sparks creativity; in an experiment published in Nature , pairs who brainstormed in person came up with about 14 percent more ideas than those brainstorming online
Face-to-face work also boosts mentorship, increasing the comments that people receive on their work by about 20 percent
Perhaps as a result, people consistently do better work when face-to-face with their colleagues and rate this work as more meaningful than work done alone
In our research, we find that having just one distant teammate weakens the connections among those sitting side by side, as team meetings move partially or fully online
Thus, any exposure to remote work in the office eliminates many benefits of the commute
Working remotely from the office has become so common because we have yet to shed two remnants of the pandemic era
The first is sprawl: Teams stretch across multiple locations
A typical team might have, say, a few employees who work in the same city, a couple who are fully remote, and one who works in a satellite office far away
So even if every teammate were in their office, the team meeting would still be largely online
During the lockdown, distance didn’t matter for jobs that could be done over Zoom
Many companies hired people far from their team’s central hub, and allowed existing employees to move farther away
In our analysis of data from one Fortune 500 firm, about 60 percent of corporate employees had at least one distant teammate after the pandemic, up from 20 percent before
Among small businesses, the distance between employees and the central office nearly tripled from 2019 to 2023, driven in large part by employees who live too far away to regularly commute to work
Many companies have simply accepted this geographic sprawl
If a team is already dispersed, managers may see nothing wrong with hiring a candidate in Detroit even though the team’s center of gravity is in Denver
Our analysis finds that job posts among Fortune 500 firms now list multiple possible office locations five times as often as a decade ago
Bad habits are another remnant of the lockdown
During COVID, many workers became accustomed to focusing on their own to-do list and churning through more tasks in less time
Now many still view in-office interactions with colleagues as distractions from their work
As they see it, going to the office means they spend time commuting just to lose more time chatting
That view misses the potential for these conversations to spark new ideas, propel others’ growth, and improve the quality of their work
Consequently, many stay home as much as they can get away with
Our analysis finds that the typical worker commutes in one fewer day than companies require: Ask for four and you get three
This might not sound like such a big deal, but on any given day, someone is likely staying home and causing their on-site peers to be on Zoom calls
When one person fails to show up, the office has less of a draw for the rest of the team

title: Nine-Inch Snails
excerpt: Since September, giant snails have put one Florida neighborhood on high alert
body: Since September, giant snails have put one Florida neighborhood on high alert

No one in a roughly 300-acre zone in the city of Hialeah, just outside of Miami, is allowed to move yard waste or even a single brick into or out of the neighborhood without explicit permission from state authorities

Teams of scientists patrol the area in search of giant African land snails, enormous mollusks with tiny teeth, a foot bigger than a 5-year-old’s, and the tendency to spread the rat-lungworm parasite, which is exactly as delightful as it sounds
The snails, which actually grow to about eight inches in length, but can stretch—if nothing else, for headline-writing purposes—to nine inches, have worried Florida authorities since 1969
Since then, the state has spent millions of dollars fending off three infestations
One such operation took a decade to complete
Now, whenever a snail is found, inspectors from the state agriculture department’s Division of Plant Industry start patrolling
They set out bait and drench hatchling-harboring soil with anti-mollusk poison

Then they distribute mug shots to the public. (That step might seem unnecessary, given that we are talking about snails the size of chipmunks, but the experts I talked with all emphasized the importance of anti-snail awareness.) An area is considered clean only after it has been monitored and treated for three years
This time, the problem “seems to be limited to just one city block,” Paul Skelley, a main architect of the agriculture department’s crackdown, told me
But the response is full-bore. “We are serious about this snail in Florida,” Skelley said. “When you find these cancers, you don’t want to let them fester
You need to cut them out.” Skelley was part of the response to the last big infestation, which lasted from 2011 until 2021, and he sounds somewhat keyed up on the phone

Giant African land snails (also known as GALS) really are giant, and meaty and sweaty-looking, like a boxer’s fist just out of the glove. “When you see the whole body out moving around,” he said, “it’s unbelievable.” Earlier this century, the International Union for Conservation of Nature declared these snails one of the worst invasive species on Earth

GALS are prevalent across a thick belt of the globe, centered on the equator, and their slime trail is widening: After expanding their range from East Africa through Madagascar, India, and the Pacific Islands, they have lately been spotted in Argentina, Beijing, and, somehow, the Italian Alps
And as climate change makes more of the world warmer and wetter, they could conquer even more territory
If the snails spread through Florida, “they could get quite a distance up the East Coast and inland” by hitching rides with humans, he said
Once they arrive somewhere new, GALS quickly multiply, and then make trouble just by being themselves
They love eating—beans, melons, ornamental flowers, shrubs—which is why they’re a hazard to agriculture
When cars run them over, the snails’ pointy shells can puncture tires
In search of minerals needed to grow their shells, they target stucco, eating our houses to build theirs
All of this can happen at a scale difficult to imagine

In the past, in Hawaii, brigades of the snails have blocked roads after rainstorms, eventually creating “a sort of mush of snail bodies and slime,” Robert Cowie, a snail researcher at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, told me. “Cars were skidding.” In Keralam, in India, where recent monsoons created the wet, humid conditions in which the snails thrive, teachers clear them daily from schools and playgrounds
In Florida, during the most recent big outbreak, Skelley’s team would purge a yard the size of a couple of parking spaces and end up pulling out maybe 2,000 snails

On their own, the African snails move as one would expect, but Skelley jokes that they can go up to 70 miles an hour—“as fast as humans can move them.” And humans—whether they’re taken in by the snails’ charisma and impressive bulk, or just unaware of the threat—like to move them
Florida’s first brush with GALS began in 1966, when a young boy brought three home from a vacation in Hawaii
His grandmother found them, the story goes, and put them out in her North Miami garden
By 1973, those three snails had become 18,000, which the state located and destroyed
Harboring the snails anywhere in the United States without a permit is illegal
Still, federal, state, and customs inspectors continue to confiscate GALS from pet owners and breeders, from schools, and from the occasional religious practitioner who (allegedly) drinks their mucus
So far, Florida’s giant-snail infestations have all been in cities and suburbs, far from farmland or protected ecosystems
But “we’re scared to death that it’s going to be found in the Everglades, some national park,” Skelley said. “That’s the worst case.” Brazil is already there
An agronomist brought the snails into the country in 1988, most likely from Indonesia, in an ill-advised attempt to create a market for giant escargot

He sold snail-rearing kits to hundreds of hopefuls, who raised GALS in their backyards. “He had a very good intention,” Silvana Thiengo, the head of the Malacology Laboratory at the Oswaldo Cruz Institute in Rio de Janeiro, told me
But unfortunately, “Brazilians are not used to eating escargot.” The snails were soon discarded on streets and in rivers
Now Thiengo receives snail specimens from around the country, and most of them are giants
They’re in urban gardens, tempting dogs to play with them; in croplands, eating bananas, beans, and soy; in the middle of the Amazon and in the country’s massive tropical wetland, the Pantanal

She and her colleagues worry about how large numbers of giant snails might compete with native species “for food, for space, for everything.” A particular worry is the rat-lungworm parasite, which can infect humans, pets, livestock, and wildlife
In humans, the worms burrow into the brain and can cause coma and death
Although the disease is quite rare, Thiengo and her colleagues have found that human cases of it have been ticking up in Brazil
But at this point, the snails are so widespread in the country that little can be done about them

title: Saudi Arabia Is Running Out of Options
excerpt: Not so long ago, the Houthi warriors who have ruled northern Yemen for the past decade seemed more like a nuisance to Saudi Arabia than a threat
body: Not so long ago, the Houthi warriors who have ruled northern Yemen for the past decade seemed more like a nuisance to Saudi Arabia than a threat
The Saudi leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, was busy glad-handing with tech bros and AI executives, talking up the kingdom’s future as a tourism destination
Then, on Saturday, a Houthi missile struck two terminals in the Saudi capital’s main airport, sending fire and smoke through the halls and causing ceiling tiles to collapse on terrified passengers
Pilgrims making their way to Mecca rolled their suitcases through trails of blood
Although Houthi strikes are not new in the kingdom, Saturday’s attack on the Riyadh airport, which killed 13 people and wounded hundreds, signaled something different
The Houthis apparently have the ability to evade the kingdom’s dwindling supply of missile interceptors by launching coordinated waves of drone swarms, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles

Saudi Arabia is now a country where the ruler must shuttle among palaces equipped with underground bunkers. “Total disbelief,” a friend in Riyadh told me. “I don’t think people thought this could happen to them.” Saudi Arabia cannot realize the crown prince’s dreams of economic and social transformation—or even continue luring foreign investors—if this kind of mayhem becomes routine

But the Houthis have become ever more intransigent, and the limits of Saudi Arabia’s ability to contain them ever more apparent. [ Read: The Houthis have a rich sense of irony and timing ] “It is starting to look as if there is no diplomatic third way,” Adam Baron, a fellow at the New America Foundation, in Washington, who specializes in Yemen and the Gulf, told me. “The Saudis will have to try to push the Houthis back militarily or accept a settlement that essentially leaves the Houthis in control of Yemen.” Both of those possibilities are risky

Experience has taught the Saudis that only a sustained ground offensive will make real headway against the Houthis, who have survived multiple bombing campaigns over the past decade, including last year’s seven-week air war by the United States
But the Saudis don’t have a ground force equal to the task
They depend on the perennially divided armed forces commanded by Yemen’s weak, internationally recognized government, based in the country’s south

Last month, the Houthis captured the area around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a crucial conduit for global oil supplies, and the Saudis responded by coordinating a new offensive to recapture the lost terrain
That effort has had mixed results; the Saudi-backed forces retook some ground, but the Houthis have unleashed a new level of firepower at the kingdom, including the strikes on the Riyadh airport
The Saudis hope to build a larger military coalition against the Houthis and have held talks with the leaders of Syria, Egypt, Pakistan, and Turkey
But those countries have made clear that their support goes only so far

They might be willing to help defend the kingdom’s borders in the event of a major ground incursion (one of the nightmare scenarios being discussed in Riyadh), but they will not become involved in a war to recapture northern Yemen
This reluctance is rooted in history: The Turks suffered legendary defeats in Yemen in the 17th and 19th centuries
Egypt got drawn into a civil war in Yemen in the 1960s—a draining conflict that has been called Egypt’s Vietnam
The Saudis could instead seek some kind of settlement with the Houthis in exchange for peace, but this seems equally elusive
The United Nations has been mediating talks in Yemen since 2012
It helped negotiate a 2022 truce that ended a seven-year war between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition
But the Houthis, who adhere to a revolutionary ideology rooted in an offshoot of Shiite Islam, have grown steadily more aggressive in their demands

Although the Houthis are fiercely independent and have their own ideas about ruling Yemen, their strategy appears to be carefully coordinated with Iran, which is still locked in its own struggle against Israel and the United States
Tehran has helped train and arm the Houthis over the years, and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps advisers are widely said to be taking part in the current fighting
The Houthis appear to be using fiber optics supplied by China to build a far more sophisticated drone force

All of this makes any kind of reliable settlement with the Houthis more difficult to achieve. [ Graeme Wood: The only thing the Houthis have done successfully ] “If you listen to the speeches by Houthi leaders, they basically say there is no such thing as Saudi Arabia—they see the kingdom as totally illegitimate and want to see it fall,” Bernard Haykel, a professor of Middle Eastern Studies at Princeton University and an expert on Saudi Arabia and Yemen, told me. “And unfortunately, they are able to draw on a deep well of resentment against the role that Saudi Arabia has historically played in Yemen.” In recent months, the Houthis have stepped up their demands, insisting that the Saudis withdraw all support from the internationally recognized government in the south, lift all sanctions, and pay reparations
But they have a long-standing habit of moving the goalposts in negotiations. “What would it take to placate the Houthis?” Haykel asked. “Can you live with them?” Many Saudis fear the answer is no
But the alternative is a war that could turn the whole country into a battleground.

title: Going Hungry in Trump’s Economy
excerpt: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
body: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
D riving through Arizona on a Saturday morning, I saw a line of cars nearly a mile long stopped along a high-desert highway
I slowed, thinking there had been an accident
Then I realized that all of those people were waiting in line for food
Weeks later, I went back to the area and met Kandy Soto
The retired administrative aide and courtroom clerk had once been a regular donor to her local food bank
But when I met her last month, she was a recipient of other people’s generosity, preparing to fill a bag with groceries that her family could no longer afford
Soto told me that the cost of canned vegetables seemed to creep up nearly every time she went to the store
After checking prices against her budget, she might buy some cheap fish fillets or canned meats, but beef or poultry were out of the question
When she voted for Donald Trump two years ago, Soto counted on him to fulfill his promise to “make America affordable again” following painful spikes in inflation under Joe Biden
She wonders what kind of life Trump and his family are living, because she sees no signs of the roaring economy he talks about
Her own family has had a run of bad luck: Her husband had to stop working after injuring his neck and requiring surgery
Then they learned that their modest retirement income made them ineligible for public assistance
All the while, prices for gas and groceries climbed

The situation grew so dire a few months ago that the 66-year-old Soto had to set aside any feelings of shame and drive 20 miles to the Community Cupboard Food Bank in Prescott. “It takes an older person a lot of giving up to do something like this,” she said
Jesse Rieser for The Atlantic The Community Cupboard in Prescott, Arizona In the surrounding county, Yavapai, Trump took 66 percent of the vote on his way to winning Arizona two years ago
In 2016, he staged a final campaign rally here before Election Day
Trump is counting on the region to help blunt what polls forecast to be a Democratic rout next month, and will hold a rally Wednesday in Bullhead City, about 200 miles to the northwest
But the president’s grip appears to be loosening, and the state of the economy explains why
The toll of rising prices has been especially acute in Arizona

About half a million residents have lost their food stamps since the summer of 2025 because of changes in Trump’s signature tax legislation, which limits assistance and penalizes states that make mistakes when they grant benefits
The law is still being phased in, and Arizona was among the first states to enact the changes
Nearly everyone I spoke with in the area last month, including Trump supporters, said they feel worse off than they were before the 2024 election
Unemployment in Arizona stood at 3.8 percent in August 2024; this August it was 4.9 percent, according to federal data
Many people I spoke with in the county said they are working, but their paychecks haven’t kept up with increased prices for gas and food
Almost all told me they are angry about Trump’s decisions to start a war and spend hundreds of millions of dollars ornamenting a capital city they will never see
They were incredulous to hear him claim that their lives have improved with him in office
Many said they are also disillusioned with Congress and with both political parties

They lamented the corruption they see as endemic in the government and in large corporations, and denounced billionaires, whom they view as capitalizing on their pain. [ Read: Trump voters are over it ] People told me they are anxious about many things: future employment opportunities, feeding their children healthy meals, keeping small businesses running, affording car repairs
Trump has said that “the American dream is back.” But not for the people I spoke with in Yavapai County
Jesse Rieser for The Atlantic A political sign at the Apache Lodge, a historic motel V ictoria Dombrowski has found a way to help her family in this economy: the barter system

She lost $800 a month in food stamps after state officials, who administer the program, took aggressive action to comply with new eligibility requirements mandated by the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Dombrowski, a stay-at-home mother of two young children, told me she had completed the renewal paperwork and had made it all the way to the end of the process, which included an interview with a caseworker about her financial situation
But even after waiting on hold for days and enlisting help from a nonprofit group, she couldn’t get through to staff at the Arizona Department of Economic Security. “And so I just gave up,” she said
I met Dombrowski at a dollar store, where she now shops because she can no longer afford Walmart
Dombrowski’s husband works at an auto-parts store, but his income isn’t enough to support the family
So she occasionally began picking up boxes of free food that were offered in the community
But more often than not, she said, the food was expired or the offerings were sugary desserts that didn’t give her kids the nutrition they needed. “My fridge is still empty,” she said
Dombrowski once prided herself on making her family hearty home-cooked food, such as meatloaf and potatoes
Since losing food aid, she has had little choice but to serve cheap microwavable meals

title: The US military’s race to make fake blood
excerpt: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2.   In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field
body: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2.   In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight

Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off.  As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher
The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move
But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board
After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground
All seven crew members were killed.   Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back

It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer
Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives
About 90% of preventable battlefield deaths are due to hemorrhage—bleeding that happens when a blood vessel ruptures—and it’s the leading cause of maternal deaths worldwide
A study published in Transfusion in 2025 found that of 1.2 million trauma patients in the United States who potentially needed blood before reaching a hospital, just 1% received it
The shortage results in about 10,000 preventable deaths each year in the US, according to the American College of Surgeons
Globally, that figure is likely in the millions .  One reason for the shortfall is that blood has a storage problem
Whole blood lasts only 35 days when refrigerated, so banks separate out components to stretch the timeline
The platelets that help wounds clot are typically stored at room temperature and last for a week or less
Hospitals and the military freeze the red blood cells that carry oxygen, as well as the protein-rich plasma that restores volume and aids coagulation

Once thawed, though, both will spoil within days. “What happens if I don’t know when I’m going to be attacked? Well, thaw it and you let it expire, right?” Murray says.  A JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests a magic number for someone who needs a transfusion: You have 36 minutes to get started
That’s why Murray—who, in addition to his military experience, has a PhD in physiology—is leading a DARPA effort to address blood’s battlefield problems
He’s in charge of a new $73 million dollar program called RAPIID (for “resuscitation and prevention of ischemia-induced dysfunction”)
Its goal is to create shelf-stable versions of the three major transfusion constituents: plasma, platelets, and red blood cells
As it gets underway late this year, RAPIID picks up on decades of work to synthesize blood or help it last longer

Most recently, that includes a prior $47.5 million DARPA project called FSHARP (for “fieldable solutions for hemorrhage with bio-artificial resuscitation products”), in which researchers have demonstrated promising results in animals.  KaloCyte techs use a device called a tangential flow filtration machine to process unencapsulated hemoglobin
MATT ROTH After processing, the hemoglobin is concentrated and then freeze-dried to make it shelf-stable
MATT ROTH With RAPIID trials for the different components occurring in parallel, the goal is to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029

That puts Murray in the position of a conductor coordinating an orchestra of clinical trials with the FDA, while also sourcing the paraphernalia that goes along with transfusions—everything from combat-durable storage bags to tests that could check how much artificial blood a patient already has.  Getting it all done will be tough, but the military is feeling the pressure to address its shortage

Blood drives may not deliver in time after a mass-casualty event, and a JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests that if the injured person needs a transfusion, the magic number is 36 minutes. “If something is survivable—and generally we classify most all hemorrhage as survivable—[you’re] almost guaranteed to survive if you get the blood before that 36-minute mark,” Murray says
After that, the chance of survival “starts to drop precipitously.”   In the mission to make portable, shelf-stable blood components, plasma is the low-hanging fruit
Researchers have known how to isolate and freeze-dry plasma, the yellowish liquid that makes up 55% of whole human blood, since the late 1930s
On the battlefields of World War II, its mix of water, salts, and thousands of types of proteins helped restore blood volume in wounded soldiers—and to some degree controlled bleeding
In the 1960s, the US abandoned freeze-dried plasma because it carried a risk of transmitting hepatitis to recipients from infected donors
But screening, testing, and drying techniques improved, and starting in 2010, the US military launched a yearslong effort to rebuild its capacity for producing these products

Over the past two years, the FDA has allowed two types of freeze-dried plasma to be used in emergencies by the US military—and one can even be used by civilians.  As for platelets, efforts at extending their life date back to the 1950s, but they haven’t seen a ton of success
Bioengineers have, for example, attempted to attach the membranes of platelets to synthetic particles
The most successful project comes from a company called Cellphire, which freeze-dries actual human platelets
The product has shown safety and efficacy in humans in clinical trials, but its dependence on donors means it’s unclear whether this approach can scale
Red blood cells have been similarly tough to preserve or mimic
Their most critical component is hemoglobin, which carries oxygen and comes encased in a cell membrane

For more than a century, researchers have been looking for ways to deliver hemoglobin without the immunological challenges created by this exterior, including the fact that donors’ and recipients’ blood types need to be compatible
Evolutionary pressure developed that wrapper for very good reason, though: “Naked” hemoglobin tends to break down quickly in the bloodstream, and that can cause organ damage
It also scavenges nitric oxide, our body’s natural mechanism for opening up blood vessels, and causes those channels to constrict

This problem became all too clear in the 1980s and 1990s, when fears that transfusions could transmit HIV sparked interest in a class of membrane-free delivery mechanisms called hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers (HBOCs)

title: Cystic fibrosis patients got their ‘miracle drug’ thanks to federal research funding – new Trump administration rules may cut future miracles short
url:
<title>Cystic fibrosis patients got their ‘miracle drug’ thanks to federal research funding – new Trump administration rules may cut future miracles short</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765950/original/file-20261013-50-gvf9n5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C25%2C5054%2C3369&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Prior to effective treatments, it was difficult for children with cystic fibrosis to live full lives.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Surf%20Therapy/b0988aeeab63430aaa4958bbef12c123/photo">Chris Carlson/AP Photo</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The hardest disease to care for when I was training <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=TLARkTcAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">as a pediatrician</a> in the late 1970s was <a href="https://www.childrenshospital.org/conditions-treatments/cystic-fibrosis">cystic fibrosis</a>, a disease in which abnormally thick mucus secretions block the lungs’ airways and make it progressively harder to breathe. </p>

<p>Back then, there was no <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0012-3692(16)62421-2">treatment for the disease</a> itself. All we had was physical therapy to clear mucus from the lungs, and drugs to dilate the airways and aid breathing. We used high doses of antibiotics to treat chronic pneumonia – drugs that also generated dangerous antibiotic-resistant infections that not only made the disease progressively harder to treat but also posed a threat to other people. At the same time, we also had to manage co-occurring conditions, including diabetes, malnutrition and heart failure.</p>

<p>Worse, these efforts did not work. In 1979 the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/archpedi.1996.02170360071012">median age of death from cystic fibrosis was 15</a>. While all young deaths are tragic, caring for children with a progressive, inevitably fatal disease that denied emerging adolescents the promise of adulthood was especially heartbreaking.</p>

<p>Cystic fibrosis treatment changed dramatically after 2012, when the biotech company Vertex Pharmaceuticals launched the drug <a href="https://www.cff.org/node/1086">Kalydeco (ivacaftor)</a>, followed by additional cystic fibrosis drugs <a href="https://www.cff.org/press-releases/2015-07/cf-foundation-celebrates-fda-approval-orkambi-important-advance-cf-community">Orkambi (lumacaftor/ivacaftor)</a> in 2015, <a href="https://www.cff.org/node/941">Symdeko (tezacaftor/ivacaftor)</a> in 2018, <a href="https://www.cff.org/press-releases/2019-10/cystic-fibrosis-foundation-statement-fda-approval-trikafta-first-triple">Trikafta (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor)</a> in 2019 and <a href="https://www.cff.org/news/2026-04/fda-approves-modulator-expansion-rare-cf-mutations">Alyftrek (vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor)</a> in 2024.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765935/original/file-20261013-60-pmrgy6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Child with nasal cannula sitting on bed, holding a doll wearing a surgical mask" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765935/original/file-20261013-60-pmrgy6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765935/original/file-20261013-60-pmrgy6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=804&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765935/original/file-20261013-60-pmrgy6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=804&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765935/original/file-20261013-60-pmrgy6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=804&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765935/original/file-20261013-60-pmrgy6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1011&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765935/original/file-20261013-60-pmrgy6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1011&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765935/original/file-20261013-60-pmrgy6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1011&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Cystic fibrosis is a fatal disease without treatment.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Panorama%20Shadow%20Buddies/1cc484148f9b490fb08821f72f551362/photo">Fernando Salazar/The Wichita Eagle via AP Photo</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Now, the median survival age for a child with cystic fibrosis <a href="https://www.cff.org/managing-cf/understanding-changes-life-expectancy">born today in the United States is 66 years</a>. Mary Vought, the former wife of the director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russell Vought, stated that their daughter, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis, “can live likely a full life because of this <a href="https://archive.li/7qAua">miracle drug</a>,” and that “it is very, very, very hopeful.” </p>

<p>Cystic fibrosis treatments are not miracles; they required decades of research funded by a combination of public and private investments. The largest contributor to this work was the National Institutes of Health, which funded much of the pivotal research required to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.2475911">understand the genetics</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM198112173052502">biology of the disease</a>. Only with this knowledge was it possible to begin searching for drugs to treat cystic fibrosis.</p>

<p>Ironically, the federal funding that was so critical to developing these drugs is now <a href="https://theconversation.com/new-trump-administration-rules-on-federal-science-funding-could-make-american-research-slower-costlier-and-harder-to-share-286430">threatened by policies</a> that were initially proposed by the Office of Management and Budget. Those policies, which would increase political control over federal research grants, limit peer review and curtail research on certain topics, were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.zcu2wsm">temporarily blocked by Congress</a>. But <a href="https://www.aau.edu/newsroom/despite-congressional-block-agencies-seek-to-implement-omb-led-grantmaking-changes">several federal agencies</a> are still pursing <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-02584-4">portions of this agenda</a>, <a href="https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-26-088.html">including the NIH</a>.</p>

<h2>NIH laid the foundation for treatment</h2>

<p>My colleagues and I examined the role that federal funding from the National Institutes of Health has played in developing cystic fibrosis treatments. We found that NIH funding supported <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamahealthforum.2023.0511">more than 6,200 published research papers</a> on the biology of cystic fibrosis in the 27 years before Kalydeco was approved in 2012. </p>

<p>Some of these publications describe celebrated milestones in understanding the biology of <em>CFTR</em> – the gene that causes cystic fibrosis – or the disease process. Others describe the studies necessary to replicate, refute or refine these advances and ensure the necessary scientific rigor to <a href="https://doi.org/10.36687/inetwp133">successfully discover and develop new drugs</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765949/original/file-20261013-50-4d2a38.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Scientist seen between stacks of lab equipment and materials" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765949/original/file-20261013-50-4d2a38.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765949/original/file-20261013-50-4d2a38.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765949/original/file-20261013-50-4d2a38.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765949/original/file-20261013-50-4d2a38.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765949/original/file-20261013-50-4d2a38.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765949/original/file-20261013-50-4d2a38.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765949/original/file-20261013-50-4d2a38.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">Decades of scientific research laid the foundation for cystic fibrosis drugs.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Overall, we identified <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamahealthforum.2023.0511">US$3.2 billion in NIH funding</a> for basic research on cystic fibrosis from 1985 to 2012 and approximately $940 million in funding for applied research on potential drugs. This funding complemented at least <a href="https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3376673">$200 million in investments</a> from the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation for the discovery or development of these drugs as well as undisclosed spending by Vertex to develop and commercialize these products. </p>

<p>The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation <a href="https://www.cff.org/press-releases/2025-02/response-to-nih-announcement-limit-funding">acknowledged the essential role of the NIH</a> in a 2025 letter to Russell Vought and other Trump administration leaders, writing that “ensuring that the National Institutes of Health (NIH) is fully functional is critical for furthering our knowledge of the biology of CF and advancing CF therapeutic development.”</p>

<h2>What will it take to produce future miracles?</h2>

<p>Developing groundbreaking drugs requires a long-term, sustained commitment from the public, from the government and from industry. </p>

<p>FDA-approved drugs are typically based on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0177371">20 to 30 years of basic research</a> in the lab and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/d41573-021-00190-9">eight to nine years</a> of human testing in the clinic. This work is supported, at least in part, by an average of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamahealthforum.2023.0511">$1.4 billion in NIH funding</a> and as much as a reported <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhealeco.2016.01.012">$1.4 billion in industry funding</a> per drug.</p>

<p>Russell Vought and his family have benefited from the commitment that scientists, advocates, legislators and industry leaders have placed into developing treatments that now offer patients with cystic fibrosis a normal life. A similar commitment can help find cures for patients who don’t respond to available drugs and to provide cures for cardiovascular disease, cancer, dementia and other conditions.</p>

<p>This commitment to research is currently under threat from Trump administration proposals that would reduce NIH funding, research, training and global research collaboration. Protecting or expanding federal funding for basic research instead can help lead to innovative therapies for countless patients.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293934/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Back then, there was no treatment for the disease itself
All we had was physical therapy to clear mucus from the lungs, and drugs to dilate the airways and aid breathing

We used high doses of antibiotics to treat chronic pneumonia – drugs that also generated dangerous antibiotic-resistant infections that not only made the disease progressively harder to treat but also posed a threat to other people
At the same time, we also had to manage co-occurring conditions, including diabetes, malnutrition and heart failure
In 1979 the median age of death from cystic fibrosis was 15
While all young deaths are tragic, caring for children with a progressive, inevitably fatal disease that denied emerging adolescents the promise of adulthood was especially heartbreaking

Cystic fibrosis treatment changed dramatically after 2012, when the biotech company Vertex Pharmaceuticals launched the drug Kalydeco (ivacaftor) , followed by additional cystic fibrosis drugs Orkambi (lumacaftor/ivacaftor) in 2015, Symdeko (tezacaftor/ivacaftor) in 2018, Trikafta (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) in 2019 and Alyftrek (vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor) in 2024
Cystic fibrosis is a fatal disease without treatment

<title>Yemen’s Houthis are bringing their war to Saudi Arabia – and reframing the narrative of being an Iranian proxy</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766177/original/file-20261014-50-axxn7v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C4368%2C2912&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Supporters of Yemen&#39;s Houthis brandish their weapons during a protest against Saudi intervention in Yemen on Oct. 8, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/supporters-of-the-houthi-authorities-brandish-their-weapons-news-photo/2298772403?phrase=houthi&amp;adppopup=true">Mohammed Huwais/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/world/middleeast/riyadh-airport-attack-energy-congress.html">deadly Houthi attack</a> on Riyadh’s international airport has highlighted how the Yemeni group is reframing its perceived “Iran proxy” role and shifting its regional focus to its ongoing battle against Saudi Arabia. The Oct. 10 strike, in which 13 people were killed and hundreds injured, was the most violent episode on Saudi Arabian soil since the beginning of the war in Iran in February. </p>

<p>It was followed by <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-13/saudi-arabia-intercepts-new-houthi-attacks-as-conflict-drags-on?cmpid=101326_morningamer&amp;utm_campaign=morningamer&amp;utm_medium=email&amp;utm_source=newsletter&amp;utm_term=261013&amp;utm_content=10016">further – albeit</a> <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/yemens-houthis-renew-warning-over-saudi-airports-after-deadly-riyadh-attack-2026-10-11/">less deadly</a> – <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/world/middleeast/saudi-arabia-yemen-houthis-aramco-threat.html">missile barrages</a> in the days since. The violence, moreover, comes just as the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/business/saudi-arabia-houthi-oil.html">kingdom is hosting a major conference</a> for oil producers. </p>

<p>As a longtime <a href="https://www.sciencespo.fr/ceri/en/directory/bonnefoy-laurent/">analyst of Yemeni politics</a>, I see the latest attacks as another illustration of both the expanding regional stalemate across the Middle East and the need to understand how Yemen’s decade-long war is having effects far beyond its territory. </p>

<h2>Houthi narratives</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://theconversation.com/who-are-yemens-houthis-106423">Houthi movement</a>  first emerged as a militarized political actor in Yemen in 2004 and has been locked in a multiyear civil war against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed central government. Currently, the Houthis control about a third of the territory and two-thirds of the population. They are undoubtedly Yemen’s most powerful armed force, despite lacking access to warplanes, and have developed an arsenal of long-range missiles and drones.       </p>

<p>All along, the Houthis have <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/uk/sectarianism-desectarianization-and-regional-politics-in-the-middle-east-9780755639212/">frequently been portrayed</a> by their adversaries and many external observers as a proxy for Iran, the chief regional rival to Saudi Arabia. </p>

<p>It’s true that the movement has <a href="https://academic.oup.com/ia/article-abstract/92/3/647/2326947">long been broadly aligned with Tehran</a> and frequently shared regional objections, <a href="https://sanaacenter.org/the-yemen-review/april-june-2026/28082">even if the relationship is complex and varied</a>. At the same time, the evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s <a href="https://hurstpublishers.com/book/tribes-and-politics-in-yemen/">domestic political context</a> and to a historical feud specific to the country – <a href="https://hurstpublishers.com/book/yemen-and-the-world/">something I and many other scholars</a> have researched.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A plume of smoke rises above a building." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766181/original/file-20261014-50-x8gsaz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766181/original/file-20261014-50-x8gsaz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766181/original/file-20261014-50-x8gsaz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766181/original/file-20261014-50-x8gsaz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766181/original/file-20261014-50-x8gsaz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766181/original/file-20261014-50-x8gsaz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766181/original/file-20261014-50-x8gsaz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A plume of smoke rises during a reported airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital of Sanaa on Oct. 9, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/plume-of-smoke-rises-during-a-reported-airstrike-by-the-news-photo/2298776531?phrase=houthi&amp;adppopup=true">AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>What is particularly significant in the current context of an escalating fight with Saudi Arabia, however, is the way in which the Houthi leadership has sought to reframe its military engagement over the course of 2026 so that it does not appear to be directed by Iran. </p>

<p>This shift is analytically important because it reveals how Houthi leaders <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/uk/huthi-movement-in-yemen-9780755644285/">understand the political effectiveness</a> of particular narratives and how they seek to legitimize their actions. </p>

<h2>A belated return to war</h2>

<p>When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, many observers expected the Houthis to enter the conflict swiftly. Their previous <a href="https://orientxxi.info/the-houthis-in-yemen-gain-the-world-s-attention,6988">intervention in the Red Sea</a> – between November 2023 and May 2025 – in support of Palestinians after Israel’s war in Gaza had, to some extent, provided a blueprint for <a href="https://atlasinstitute.org/the-red-sea-shipping-crisis-2024-2025-houthi-attacks-and-global-trade-disruption/">disrupting maritime traffic</a> through the Strait of Hormuz. </p>

<p>The symbolic returns of their earlier campaign had been considerable. On the one hand, it demonstrated the Houthis’ willingness to act in support of Gaza at a time when many Arab governments were <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/6/29/why-the-arab-league-could-not-stop-israels-genocide">widely perceived as turning their backs</a> on the plight of Palestinians. It also revealed the movement’s capacity to disrupt global supply chains and affect international trade far beyond Yemen.</p>

<p>But the Houthis remained on the sidelines for several months after the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Their leaders appeared to disregard reports that Iranian decision-makers <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/iran-tells-houthis-close-red-sea-gateway-if-us-hits-power-network-sources-say-2026-07-16/">had called on them</a>, in July 2026, to close the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to maritime traffic.</p>

<p>Assuming that the Houthis would automatically act at Tehran’s command reflected a misreading of Yemeni history and of the identity markers that shape the movement’s political legitimacy. Acting in support of Palestinians could be framed for a domestic and regional audience as an expression of Arab solidarity. But acting on behalf of Iran, a non-Arab Persian country composed almost entirely of <a href="https://theconversation.com/twelver-shiism-a-branch-of-islam-that-serves-both-as-a-spiritual-and-political-force-in-iran-and-beyond-259853">Twelver Shia Muslims</a>, was considerably more difficult to rationalize in Arab Yemen where Twelver Shia Muslims are absent and Sunnis are the majority. </p>

<p>The Houthis’ reentry into the regional conflict in August took place alongside a shift in their political narrative, which increasingly centered on their long-standing adversary, Saudi Arabia. </p>

<p>Although the strategic consequences of their actions may ultimately benefit Iran in its own regional and international conflicts, the Houthis see their military campaign against Saudi Arabia chiefly as an act of national defense.</p>

<h2>An earlier airport bombing</h2>

<p>During the summer of 2026, an important episode went largely unnoticed in the Western media: the Houthis’ attempt to <a href="https://sanaacenter.org/publications/perspectives-and-analyses/27981">establish the reopening</a> of Sanaa International Airport through the surprise departure of a Tehran-bound flight and its subsequent return.</p>

<p>The airport, located in the Houthi-controlled capital, had been closed since late 2024 following <a href="https://www.newarab.com/news/israeli-strikes-shut-down-sanaa-airport-cause-500m-damages">Israeli strikes</a>. Its continued closure meant that access to and exit from Houthi-controlled territory remained subject to restrictions imposed by the movement’s adversaries. These included the authorities controlling Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognized government.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A man walks by the shell of a destroyed airplane fuselage." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766180/original/file-20261014-50-p512o4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766180/original/file-20261014-50-p512o4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766180/original/file-20261014-50-p512o4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766180/original/file-20261014-50-p512o4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766180/original/file-20261014-50-p512o4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766180/original/file-20261014-50-p512o4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766180/original/file-20261014-50-p512o4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">An airport official walks past the wreckage of a military transport aircraft destroyed by Saudi-led airstrikes at Sanaa’s airport in 2015.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=saudi%20bombing%20yemen%202015&amp;mediaType=photo">AP Photo/Hani Mohammed</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>From the Houthis’ perspective, their sovereignty consequently remained incomplete. The airport’s closure not only restricted civilian movement but also limited their ability to send supporters abroad for training and potentially to receive military equipment. On July 13, the Saudi military’s <a href="https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/moment-iranian-plane-lands-in-yemens-hudaydah-after-strike-on-sanaa-airport-2/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX09XQU5BQ0FBVklERU8yMDI2MDcxMzQxOTY1NDY4">subsequent bombing</a> of the Sanaa runway, as the incoming aircraft from Tehran approached, provided the movement an opportunity to reignite its confrontation with Riyadh.</p>

<p>After more than three years of a de facto ceasefire and difficult negotiations, Riyadh appeared, as in its dealings with Iran, <a href="https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/middle-east-north-africa/yemen-saudi-arabia/yemens-war-returning">increasingly eager to extricate itself</a> from the region’s protracted conflicts. Sensing an opening, the Houthi leadership responded by invoking a logic of tit-for-tat retaliation. </p>

<p>The Houthis’ tactics today are a kind of mirror to the <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-29319423">2015 launch of a Saudi-led bombing campaign</a> and blockade of the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen that has led to years of protracted civil war. The Houthis now claim the right to impose reciprocal restrictions on Saudi Arabia, particularly by targeting its ports and oil-exporting infrastructure.</p>

<h2>Saudi’s Houthi blowback</h2>

<p>The Houthis’ new tactic serves two purposes. First, it allows the Houthis to <a href="https://sanaacenter.org/publications/perspectives-and-analyses/28309">redirect responsibility</a> for the economic and humanitarian crisis in and around Sanaa toward the Saudi-enforced blockade rather than their own governance failures, mismanagement and corruption. Second, it provides a rationale for escalating the conflict across the region.</p>

<p>Previously, the Houthi military leadership had <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/11/11/yemens-houthis-appear-to-pull-back-from-red-sea-shipping-attacks">halted attacks</a> on Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea following the formal Gaza ceasefire of October 2025, despite having repeatedly come under bombardment. It had likewise suspended attacks on American vessels following an <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/trump-says-us-will-stop-bombing-houthis-after-agreement-struck-2025-05-06/">agreement with the Trump administration</a> in May 2025.</p>

<p>These decisions demonstrated a <a href="https://theconversation.com/america-is-the-mother-of-terrorism-why-the-houthis-new-slogan-is-important-for-understanding-the-middle-east-222865">degree of pragmatism</a> beneath the movement’s inflammatory rhetoric. That pragmatism appeared to persist even as the Houthis resumed their regional military engagement, with American diplomats reportedly <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/us-officials-met-iran-backed-houthis-oman-over-weekend-sources-say-2026-09-16/">meeting Houthi representatives in Oman</a> in September 2026. </p>

<p><iframe id="7bAJT" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/7bAJT/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of the Persian Gulf region"></iframe></p>

<p>With Saudi Arabia, however, the Houthis felt less compunction. Riyadh was already facing repeated barrages of Iran missiles as a consequences of its alliance with the U.S. and facing an energy export squeeze. So with the Saudi airport incident, the Houthi leadership feels it <a href="https://theconversation.com/rapid-houthi-advances-in-yemen-pose-massive-strategic-risks-for-saudi-arabia-in-the-gulf-292070">has trapped Saudi Arabia</a>, with consequences extending to the global economy.</p>

<p>This retaliatory strategy was bolstered by <a href="https://sanaacenter.org/publications/perspectives-and-analyses/28317">successful Houthi moves</a> in early September to establish a degree of control over the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime choke points. That gave the Houthis leverage over shipping crucial for Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.</p>

<p>Drones and ballistic missiles, as the attacks on the Riyadh airport illustrate, also give the movement the <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/11/why-are-houthi-missiles-breaking-through-saudi-arabias-air-defences">capacity to strike targets</a> across much of Saudi Arabia.</p>

<p>The targeting of civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, particularly airports, illustrates the retaliatory logic the Houthis have invoked to justify their actions.</p>

<p>It’s far from clear what the consequences of this increasingly aggressive Houthi campaign will be. The region seems poised for ongoing strife, and it’s an open question whether it will draw back in the likes of the U.S., which has been reluctant to return to full-scale regional conflict.</p>

<p>Yet none of that should obscure the plight of civilians in Yemen. Rather, it should serve as a reminder of the suffering of a population exhausted by a war that has lasted for more than a decade and has devastated the already meager infrastructure of <a href="https://saqibooks.com/books/saqi/yemen-in-crisis/">what was the poorest country</a> in the Middle East even before the conflict started.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294208/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

All along, the Houthis have frequently been portrayed by their adversaries and many external observers as a proxy for Iran, the chief regional rival to Saudi Arabia
It’s true that the movement has long been broadly aligned with Tehran and frequently shared regional objections, even if the relationship is complex and varied

At the same time, the evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country – something I and many other scholars have researched
A plume of smoke rises during a reported airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital of Sanaa on Oct. 9, 2026

AFP via Getty Images What is particularly significant in the current context of an escalating fight with Saudi Arabia, however, is the way in which the Houthi leadership has sought to reframe its military engagement over the course of 2026 so that it does not appear to be directed by Iran
This shift is analytically important because it reveals how Houthi leaders understand the political effectiveness of particular narratives and how they seek to legitimize their actions
A belated return to war When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, many observers expected the Houthis to enter the conflict swiftly

Their previous intervention in the Red Sea – between November 2023 and May 2025 – in support of Palestinians after Israel’s war in Gaza had, to some extent, provided a blueprint for disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz
The symbolic returns of their earlier campaign had been considerable
On the one hand, it demonstrated the Houthis’ willingness to act in support of Gaza at a time when many Arab governments were widely perceived as turning their backs on the plight of Palestinians
It also revealed the movement’s capacity to disrupt global supply chains and affect international trade far beyond Yemen
But the Houthis remained on the sidelines for several months after the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran
Their leaders appeared to disregard reports that Iranian decision-makers had called on them , in July 2026, to close the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to maritime traffic
Assuming that the Houthis would automatically act at Tehran’s command reflected a misreading of Yemeni history and of the identity markers that shape the movement’s political legitimacy
Acting in support of Palestinians could be framed for a domestic and regional audience as an expression of Arab solidarity

But acting on behalf of Iran, a non-Arab Persian country composed almost entirely of Twelver Shia Muslims , was considerably more difficult to rationalize in Arab Yemen where Twelver Shia Muslims are absent and Sunnis are the majority
The Houthis’ reentry into the regional conflict in August took place alongside a shift in their political narrative, which increasingly centered on their long-standing adversary, Saudi Arabia

Although the strategic consequences of their actions may ultimately benefit Iran in its own regional and international conflicts, the Houthis see their military campaign against Saudi Arabia chiefly as an act of national defense

An earlier airport bombing During the summer of 2026, an important episode went largely unnoticed in the Western media: the Houthis’ attempt to establish the reopening of Sanaa International Airport through the surprise departure of a Tehran-bound flight and its subsequent return
The airport, located in the Houthi-controlled capital, had been closed since late 2024 following Israeli strikes
Its continued closure meant that access to and exit from Houthi-controlled territory remained subject to restrictions imposed by the movement’s adversaries
These included the authorities controlling Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognized government
An airport official walks past the wreckage of a military transport aircraft destroyed by Saudi-led airstrikes at Sanaa’s airport in 2015
AP Photo/Hani Mohammed From the Houthis’ perspective, their sovereignty consequently remained incomplete
The airport’s closure not only restricted civilian movement but also limited their ability to send supporters abroad for training and potentially to receive military equipment

On July 13, the Saudi military’s subsequent bombing of the Sanaa runway, as the incoming aircraft from Tehran approached, provided the movement an opportunity to reignite its confrontation with Riyadh

After more than three years of a de facto ceasefire and difficult negotiations, Riyadh appeared, as in its dealings with Iran, increasingly eager to extricate itself from the region’s protracted conflicts
Sensing an opening, the Houthi leadership responded by invoking a logic of tit-for-tat retaliation
The Houthis’ tactics today are a kind of mirror to the 2015 launch of a Saudi-led bombing campaign and blockade of the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen that has led to years of protracted civil war
The Houthis now claim the right to impose reciprocal restrictions on Saudi Arabia, particularly by targeting its ports and oil-exporting infrastructure
