<title>Philly voters care about local issues, but election integrity fears make them wonder if their vote matters</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764981/original/file-20261008-50-vm50dv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5160%2C3440&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Philadelphia voters will help elect the state&#39;s next governor and lieutenant governor, as well as members of the U.S. House of Representatives and the state Legislature, in the 2026 midterms.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/sign-encouraging-people-to-vote-hangs-from-the-facade-of-a-news-photo/2182431281">Matthew Hatcher/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Less than 30 days ahead of the 2026 midterms and almost nobody I talk to in Philadelphia is excited. Not my neighbors. Not my students or colleagues at Temple University, where I research and teach <a href="https://klein.temple.edu/directory/heather-lamarre-tuf30092">political communication and public opinion</a>. Not even my politically engaged friends. </p>

<p>This mirrors the national mood in recent years: In a <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/americans-dismal-views-of-the-nations-politics/">Pew Research Center survey</a>, just 4% of Americans said they feel excited about politics; 65% said they feel exhausted. </p>

<p>“There are many factors that go into voter apathy,” explains Temple University political communications professor Bruce Hardy, “barriers to participation, lack of trust, cynicism, sense of disenfranchisement and powerlessness, political fatigue, and so on.” </p>

<p>Voter malaise and campaign fatigue aren’t new, but something feels different to me this time. </p>

<p>Lauren Cristella, president and CEO of the <a href="https://seventy.org/">Committee of Seventy</a>, a nonpartisan organization established to improve the voting process and engage Philadelphia citizens in the democratic process, agrees. She points to election integrity fears being hotly debated in the national media as part of the problem. </p>

<p>“We are sitting on the back side of a <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/404240/americans-thought-enthusiasm-midterms-down-2018.aspx">big decline in voter enthusiasm</a>,” she said, “And yes, we need to start giving voters something to be excited about. However, what we are seeing in the commonwealth is a lot of confusion and fear around election integrity.” </p>

<p>This tension, in my view, is the real story of the 2026 midterms. Voters still care. The stakes are higher than ever. But the question on many voters’ minds is: Will my vote even count?  </p>

Vote Early!'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764994/original/file-20261008-60-fqi6yk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764994/original/file-20261008-60-fqi6yk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764994/original/file-20261008-60-fqi6yk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764994/original/file-20261008-60-fqi6yk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764994/original/file-20261008-60-fqi6yk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764994/original/file-20261008-60-fqi6yk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764994/original/file-20261008-60-fqi6yk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Philadelphia residents wait in a line around City Hall to cast their ballot on the last day of early voting on Oct. 29, 2024.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/philadelphia-residents-wait-in-a-line-around-city-hall-to-news-photo/2181171514">Photo by Matthew Hatcher/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Election integrity fears are widespread</h2>

<p>This is not just a Philadelphia problem. A July 2026 <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/712955/election-concerns-run-high-ahead-2026-midterms.aspx">Gallup survey</a> of more than 23,000 adults found that 2 in 3 Americans were concerned about political leaders pressuring election officials to change outcomes. Half worried that their own ballot would not be counted. </p>

<p>Voter confidence is sliding. In a 2026 <a href="https://elections.ucsd.edu/_files/surveys/Trust-in-Elections-Sept-2026.pdf">University of California San Diego survey</a>, 49% of Americans said they expect the midterms to be free and fair, while 51% expect unfair elections or aren’t sure. </p>

<p>A 2026 Pew survey similarly found that <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/08/05/how-confident-are-americans-in-the-midterm-elections-fairness-and-accuracy/">barely half of Americans are confident</a> that November’s midterm elections will be conducted fairly and accurately. This represents a 10-point drop in national voter confidence from 61% in the 2024 elections. </p>

<h2>Gap between democratic attitudes and voting behavior</h2>

<p>Social and behavioral scientists have long understood the tension between one’s beliefs and attitudes about voting: For example, many people say they believe voting is an important democratic behavior, but then don’t actually vote themselves. </p>

<p>Efforts to close the gap between people’s intentions to vote and getting them to actually vote are where issues like <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/736867">mail-in voting</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/736867">polling locations</a>, <a href="https://publications.lawschool.cornell.edu/jlpp/2023/01/20/the-case-for-making-election-day-a-federal-holiday/">time off work</a> and <a href="https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification">voter ID laws</a> make a difference. </p>

<p>Voting by mail has been a flash point since the 2020 presidential election when <a href="https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/local/dueling-vote-counting-demonstrations-outside-philadelphias-tally-center/2586922/">Philadelphia and Pennsylvania sat at the center of controversy</a>. However, this <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/vote/elections/fact-checking-pa-related-election-claims">should not be an issue</a> for Philadelphians – or Pennsylvanians – in the upcoming midterms. The U.S. Supreme Court recently <a href="https://keystonenewsroom.com/news/elections/mail-voting-is-underway-in-pennsylvania-heres-what-to-know/">blocked a federal attempt</a> to impose new Postal Service rules limiting mail-in voting. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Protesters outside wearing masks hold signs that say 'Count every vote'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764995/original/file-20261008-60-i6shdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764995/original/file-20261008-60-i6shdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764995/original/file-20261008-60-i6shdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764995/original/file-20261008-60-i6shdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764995/original/file-20261008-60-i6shdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764995/original/file-20261008-60-i6shdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764995/original/file-20261008-60-i6shdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Cristella told me that mail-in voting is “the safest and most secure of any time in the commonwealth’s history.” Every <a href="https://www.pavoterservices.pa.gov/pages/ballottracking.aspx">ballot can be tracked</a>. </p>

<p>So why are Pennsylvania voters not convinced? </p>

<h2>‘What’s the point?’ is a rational response</h2>

<p>A 2021 article <a href="https://now.tufts.edu/2021/11/02/how-much-do-doubts-about-election-fairness-affect-voting-and-democracy">that cites experts at Tufts University</a> explains how pushing myths like the “election was stolen” or “the election wasn’t fair” – presumably to explain away Donald Trump’s loss in 2020 and create mobilization for his 2024 presidential run – can boomerang and end up lowering confidence in future elections. </p>

<p>If people don’t believe their vote will count, then it becomes completely rational to simultaneously hold the opinion that voting is generally good for democracy, while also lacking any faith that their own vote will even be counted. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Experts say negative national media coverage of politics can leave voters feeling cynical about local elections too.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/voter-shows-off-their-sticker-after-casting-their-ballots-news-photo/2276547015">Matthew Hatcher/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1460-2466.1999.tb02784.x">Framing theory</a> explains how the presentation of information in the media influences the way people process and interpret it. </p>

<p>Hardy attributes much of the current state of voter apathy to the media’s focus on fraud and voter integrity. He says that “much of this comes from political discourse and media focusing on national political conflict, a seemingly endless election cycle, and a constant reinforcement of political in-groups and out-groups.” </p>

<p>Even though our elections are safe and secure in Philadelphia, he explains, “All of this negative national media coverage can overshadow the importance of local elections and leave people feeling disengaged from the politics closest to home.” </p>

<p>Cristella agrees that media framing is a significant part of the problem.</p>

<p>“Issues surrounding election fraud and vote integrity get amplified and muddied,” she said. When isolated issues in other states occur, even if proved untrue, the intense and repeated national media attention on them shakes voter confidence here at home.  </p>

<h2>What this means for Philly</h2>

<p>The 2026 midterms will be an <a href="https://whyy.org/articles/election-2026-pennsylvania-young-voters-guide/">important election</a> for Pennsylvania, as the election will determine the state’s next governor and lieutenant governor, as well as members of the U.S. House of Representatives and the state Legislature.</p>

<p>Philadelphians have a lot on the line. </p>

<p>Economic concerns, in particular, are a major issue this election. A recent <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/1675/most-important-problem.aspx">Gallup poll</a> indicates that confidence in the economy is at its weakest level since 2022. And the voters are feeling the pinch.</p>

<p>While the <a href="https://vote-results.phila.gov/ResultsSW.aspx?type=WEC&amp;Area=43&amp;map=CTY">2026 Philadelphia primary had a low 22% turnout</a>, Cristella believes issues like affordability will lead to a strong turnout in November. </p>

<p>As a longtime Philadelphian who believes strongly in our democracy, I am staying hopeful. </p>

<title>Republicans can confirm a Supreme Court justice if Democrats take the Senate, but at what cost?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765869/original/file-20261013-50-4t7hyi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5111%2C3407&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Democrats will attempt to slow down the confirmation process, but they face an uphill battle with few options.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/view-of-columns-royalty-free-image/1135798009?phrase=Supreme%20Court%20Congress%20US&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Grant Faint/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://www.cookpolitical.com/ratings/senate-race-ratings">Democrats are gaining momentum</a> in <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/10/04/2026-midterm-election-betting-odds-house-senate/92092792007/">their bid</a> to <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/senate-polls-2026.html">retake the Senate in November</a>. This has led Republicans to prepare for the possibility that <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/07/senate-supreme-court-lame-duck-01109203">a conservative Supreme Court justice</a> might announce their retirement before the new Congress is sworn in on <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RL30725">Jan. 3, 2027</a>.</p>

<p>This would give President Donald Trump his fourth Supreme Court nomination, helping to ensure conservative dominance on the court for decades.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Kdr4x8oAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Supreme Court scholar</a>, I know that judicial appointments have real consequences. Look no further than <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1971/70-18">Roe v. Wade</a>: Within two years of securing a 6–3 conservative majority, the high court in 2022 eliminated the constitutional right to abortion that had existed for almost 50 years.</p>

<p>If Democrats take over the Senate and a Republican-appointed justice retires before Jan. 3, this will trigger one of the most explosive confirmation battles in American history.</p>

<p>Here’s how the fight is likely to play out – and why the stakes are so high.</p>

<h2>Who is most likely to retire?</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/democrats-dont-expect-fill-supreme-court-vacancy-trump-rcna600908">Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas</a> top <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/04/supreme-court-justice-alito-thought-about-retiring.html">the list of potential retirees</a> should Democrats win the Senate in November. Alito and Thomas are the court’s oldest justices, at 76 and 78, respectively. Thomas is also the court’s longest-serving justice, appointed by President George H.W. Bush in 1991.</p>

<p>Perhaps more importantly, both justices have <a href="https://www.propublica.org/series/supreme-court-scotus">deep ties</a> to the <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-the-conservative-federalist-society-will-affect-the-supreme-court-for-decades-to-come-263397">conservative legal movement</a>. This is a network of lawyers, judges and politicians who seek to etch conservative principles into law. Overturning Roe v. Wade was at the top of the conservative <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-conservative-groups-will-advance-their-agendas-before-a-supreme-court-with-amy-coney-barrett-147084">wish list</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0329692">My research suggests</a> that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139626453">both Alito and Thomas care about their legacies</a>. And they both understand that a Democratic-controlled Senate would block another Trump-appointed nominee.</p>

<p>Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/democrats-dont-expect-fill-supreme-court-vacancy-trump-rcna600908">made this clear</a> on Oct. 5, 2026, as did Senate Judiciary Committee member Richard Blumenthal, the Democrat from Connecticut. <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/democrats-dont-expect-fill-supreme-court-vacancy-trump-rcna600908">Blumenthal said</a>, “It is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration.”</p>

<p>Though Alito has recently indicated <a href="https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/10/06/congress/alito-retirement-lame-duck-01108410">he intends to stay on the court</a> through its 2026 term, Thomas has made no recent public statements about retirement. And Alito is free to change his mind at any time.</p>

<p>If Alito or Thomas announced their retirement after the midterms, Republicans would have enough time to confirm a successor. The Senate has <a href="https://www.senate.gov/legislative/resources/pdf/2026_calendar.pdf">four and a half work weeks scheduled</a> between Election Day and Jan. 3. Justice Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12679">less than a month</a> after her nomination, making the timeline tight but doable.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman in a burgundy dress stands in front of a table and raises her right hand while several people wearing masks look on." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=361&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=361&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=361&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=453&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=453&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765874/original/file-20261013-50-2yccx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=453&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/supreme-court-justice-nominee-judge-amy-coney-barrett-news-photo/1229032886?phrase=Amy%20Coney%20Barrett%20confirmation&amp;adppopup=true">Shawn Thew-Pool/Getty Images</a></span>

<p>Democrats will likely attempt to slow down the process, but they face an uphill battle with few options. <a href="https://time.com/4728558/neil-gorsuch-filibuster-senate-confirmation-vote/">Republicans stripped away key delaying tactics</a> in recent years by ending the filibuster in 2017 <a href="https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/press/rep/releases/senate-judiciary-committee-unanimously-sends-judge-barretts-nomination-to-the-full-senate">and ignoring</a> the <a href="https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/about/committee/rules">Judiciary Committee’s quorum rules</a> in 2020. This rule requires nine members be present to transact business, including two members of the minority party. </p>

<h2>A potentially historic battle</h2>

<p>A Republican effort to confirm a Supreme Court nominee during a lame-duck Senate would spark a historic battle with Democrats.</p>

<p>Democrats would surely point to how Republicans handled <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/president-obama-nominate-merrick-garland-supreme-court/story?id=37633715">President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland</a> in 2016. A seat on the court opened up <a href="https://www.npr.org/2016/02/13/140647230/justice-antonin-scalia-known-for-biting-dissents-dies-at-79">after conservative Antonin Scalia died</a> on Feb. 13, almost nine months before the November presidential election.</p>

<p>Republicans refused to move Garland’s nomination through the confirmation process, using their majority power to <a href="https://apnews.com/united-states-government-2d97d3c84cc445dc9e09a8406d901765">set the Senate’s agenda</a>. This marked the first time since 1866 that <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/history-stolen-supreme-court-seats-180962589/">a Supreme Court nomination that was not withdrawn</a> failed to receive an up-or-down vote in the Senate.</p>

<p>To justify this, Republicans created the so-called “<a href="https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/1464958/mitch-mcconnell-explains-his-rule-for-holding-supreme-court-vacancies-open/">McConnell Rule</a>,” named after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky. According to <a href="https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/1464958/mitch-mcconnell-explains-his-rule-for-holding-supreme-court-vacancies-open/">McConnell</a>, the Senate should not fill Supreme Court vacancies “in the middle of a presidential election year.” </p>

<p>Four years later, Senate Republicans abruptly <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/27/us/mcconnell-barrett-confirmation.html">abandoned the rule</a>. This allowed them to push through Coney Barrett’s confirmation just days before the 2020 presidential election.</p>

<p>Democrats did not take kindly to this reversal.</p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer speaks in front of the U.S. Capitol after a boycott of the Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on the nomination of Judge Amy Coney Barrett to the U.S. Supreme Court on Oct. 22, 2020.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/minority-leader-sen-chuck-schumer-speaks-as-sen-dianne-news-photo/1281651759?phrase=Senate%20Minority%20Leader%20Chuck%20Schumer%20October%202020&amp;adppopup=true">Alex Wong/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Schumer pulled no punches in a speech the day of Barrett’s confirmation vote. Schumer <a href="https://www.democrats.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/schumer-floor-remarks-on-the-nomination-of-judge-amy-coney-barrett-to-the-united-states-supreme-court">said</a> the day “will go down as one of the darkest days in the 231-year history of the United States Senate.”</p>

<p>He alleged the Republican majority made “a mockery of its own stated principle – that the American people deserve a voice in the selection of Supreme Court Justices – completing the partisan theft of two seats on the Supreme Court using completely contradictory rationales.”</p>

<p>Democrats were clearly outraged by what they saw as two stolen Supreme Court seats.</p>

<p>However, I believe that pushing through a nominee will trigger an even fiercer fight. Senate Democrats will see such a confirmation as a power grab that sidelines the voice of voters.</p>

<p>Furthermore, if a Republican justice retires should Democrats win the Senate, the move will almost certainly be viewed as purely partisan.</p>

<p>This has the potential to further <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.12820">erode public support</a> for <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/4732/supreme-court.aspx">the court</a>, which is sitting <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/07/30/favorable-views-of-supreme-court-remain-near-historic-low/">near historic lows</a>. And it will likely fuel the fire of Supreme Court reform, including the possibility of <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/supreme-court-reform-gathers-momentum">expanding the number of justices on the court</a>.</p>

<p>Put simply, in securing a short-term conservative victory, Republicans may end up handing Democrats the exact justification they need to reshape the high court.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293778/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>In newly independent US, Americans debated whether public executions taught a lesson or just showed off the state’s power to destroy</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765958/original/file-20261013-50-bzz96t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C13%2C3669%2C2446&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A 1747 print of a public execution at the so-called Tyburn Tree, a gallows in London that served for hundreds of years as a site of hangings.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/399844">William Hogarth</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The proposed <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/08/politics/pete-hegseth-vows-to-make-first-firing-squad-execution-in-decades-public">livestream of Nidal Hasan’s execution</a> by a U.S. military firing squad gives an old question a new audience. Hasan, an Army psychiatrist convicted by a military court of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, is scheduled to be executed on Dec. 3, 2026.</p>

<p>Explaining the plan to make his death public, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that “people need to understand … <a href="https://edition.cnn.com/2026/10/09/politics/fort-hood-execution-hegseth-livestream">there’s serious consequences for these types of things</a>.”</p>

<p>Whether the broadcast will proceed remains uncertain. But <a href="https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/videos/maurizio-valsania-first-among-men-george-washington-and-myth-american">as a historian of the early American republic</a>, I recognize a familiar expectation behind it: that watching someone die will teach a useful lesson. Americans at the republic’s founding debated that premise — and doubted what the lesson might be.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/nOxz2S7-oMY?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution of Nidal Hasan will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The power of government</h2>

<p>On Aug. 17, 1797, New Yorkers gathered to watch John Young hang.</p>

<p>An English musician and music publisher struggling with debt, <a href="https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=coo.31924109046239&amp;seq=1">Young had shot and killed Robert Barwick</a>, a deputy sheriff taking him into custody. Barwick left a widow and nine children. </p>

<p><a href="https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/evans/N24300.0001.001/?view=toc">Young’s conviction by a jury</a> brought him to a scaffold surrounded by soldiers, before an immense crowd. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.nga.org/governor/john-jay/">Governor John Jay</a>, a leading Federalist who placed greater faith in firm government than in popular judgment, had authorized the military presence after the sheriff reported fears of a rescue. But Jay also wanted the execution to impress its witnesses with the power of the government carrying it out.</p>

<p>Writing to <a href="https://history.nycourts.gov/figure/james-kent/">James Kent</a>, New York City’s chief municipal legal officer, two days before the hanging, Jay stressed that the authority of law should prevail visibly. The occasion should be “particularly solemn and impressive,” he said. The “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511844997">authority of the law should be seen to bear down (on) all opposition</a>.”</p>

<p>Solemnity, however, proved difficult to arrange. The military escort played lively music as the procession made its way to the scaffold. One newspaper critic thought an uninformed passerby might mistake the spectacle for “<a href="https://infoweb-newsbank-com.tjportal.idm.oclc.org/apps/readex/doc?p=EANX&amp;t=pubname%3A10D345D01D2428C8%21New-York%2BGazette/year%3A1797%211797/mody%3A0818%21August%2B18&amp;year=1797&amp;docref=image/v2%3A10D345D01D2428C8%40EANX-1197270C5729F268%402377631-1197270C79D1FC98%401&amp;origin=image/v2%3A10D345D01D2428C8%40EANX-1197270C5729F268%402377631-1197270C71D89AD8%400">the celebration of some Festival</a>.”</p>

<p>Soldiers formed a square around the gallows. The crowd remained orderly. Young addressed a few words to the minister, sang a psalm “<a href="https://infoweb-newsbank-com.tjportal.idm.oclc.org/apps/readex/doc?p=EANX&amp;t=pubname%3A109215B64EAFB460%21Greenleaf%2527s%2BNew%2BYork%2BJournal/year%3A1797%211797/mody%3A0819%210819&amp;sort=YMD_date%3AA&amp;fld-base-0=alltext&amp;val-base-0=young&amp;docref=image/v2%3A109215B64EAFB460%40EANX-1095B8A2EA913398%402377632-1095B8A604F62058%402-1095B8A8360C3268%40Friday%252C%2BAugust.%2B18&amp;firsthit=yes">and with great composure pulled his cap over his face</a>,” reported one newspaper. Then, before the assembled witnesses, he was hanged.</p>



<h2>Loss of government’s dignity</h2>

<p>Whatever the crowd’s reaction that day, the public execution had already become <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/rites-of-execution-9780195066630?cc=ch&amp;lang=en&amp;">an argument about the nature of government</a>.</p>

<p>The display did not impress everyone as evidence of governmental strength. Writing in the “Greenleaf’s New York Journal” two weeks after the hanging, “A CITIZEN” accused Jay of “letting down the dignity of civil authority.” Calling out troops for the execution suggested, among other things, “<a href="https://infoweb-newsbank-com.tjportal.idm.oclc.org/apps/readex/doc?p=EANX&amp;t=pubname%3A109215B64EAFB460%21Greenleaf%2527s%2BNew%2BYork%2BJournal/year%3A1797%211797/mody%3A0830%210830&amp;sort=YMD_date%3AA&amp;fld-base-0=alltext&amp;val-base-0=executive&amp;val-database-0=&amp;fld-database-0=database&amp;fld-nav-0=YMD_date&amp;val-nav-0=&amp;docref=image/v2%3A109215B64EAFB460%40EANX-1095B8BF32F07B48%402377643-1095B8C1EB7B7070%403-1095B8C3EFC92B68%40For%2Bthe%2BArgus.%2BTo%2BJohn%2BJay%252C%2BGovernor%2Bof%2Bthe%2BState%2Bof%2BNew-York&amp;firsthit=yes">a wantonness on the part of the Executive</a>.”</p>

<p>To this critic, the military presence advertised executive excess. The spectacle could undermine the very authority it was meant to affirm.</p>

<p>That point mattered in a republic still deciding how its authority should differ from that of the European monarchies that Americans portrayed as corrupt.</p>

<p>In the 1780s and 1790s, American reformers took particular aim at England’s “<a href="https://msupress.org/9781611865370/executing-democracy/">sanguinary laws</a>” – statutes prescribing death for offenses ranging from murder to relatively minor theft.</p>

<p>By 1776, nearly 200 offenses carried a possible death sentence in England. These laws had accumulated piecemeal over generations, but American critics portrayed them as a single system with bloodshed at its center.</p>

<p>England’s punishments became a measure of what republican justice must overcome. Independence required Americans to reconsider how readily, and under what circumstances, <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674010833">their own governments could take a life</a>.</p>

<p>The contrast was partly an exercise in national self-definition. Americans cast English severity as evidence of <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/7313/to-begin-the-world-anew-by-bernard-bailyn/">an old, corrupt political order</a> and imagined their own laws as rational, proportionate and suited to free citizens. </p>

<p>In practice, the distinction was harder to sustain.</p>

<p>Nevertheless, the aspiration entered constitutional language. New Hampshire’s 1784 Constitution declared a multitude of sanguinary laws “both impolitic and unjust.” Punishment’s proper object was “<a href="https://law.justia.com/constitution/new-hampshire/billofrights.html">to reform, not to exterminate mankind</a>.”</p>

<p>Reform did not necessarily mean abolition. In 1796, New York reduced the number of crimes punishable by death but <a href="https://www.nycourts.gov/courts/ad4/library/pdfs/deathpenalty.pdf">retained capital punishment for murder</a>.</p>

<p>Young went to the gallows the following year. Even if Jay favored milder criminal laws, he was able to see a carefully staged execution as a necessary assertion of public authority. </p>

<h2>No guarantee of lesson learned</h2>

<p>Other Americans pressed further. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Benjamin-Rush">Benjamin Rush</a>, the Philadelphia physician and signer of the Declaration of Independence, opposed executing even murderers. His argument went to the heart of the relationship between government and the governed. </p>

<p>“Capital punishments are the natural offspring of monarchical governments,” <a href="https://press-pubs.uchicago.edu/founders/documents/amendVIIIs16.html">Rush wrote in 1792</a>. “Kings consider their subjects as their property.”</p>

<p>For Rush, a republic that put citizens to death still acted like a monarchy, treating citizens’ lives as its own to dispose of. Calling the killing a lawful punishment did not make it less an act of revenge.</p>

<p>A related debate concerned the audience. Even Americans who accepted capital punishment could doubt the wisdom of making it public.</p>

<p>In 1787, Rush had already questioned what spectators actually learned from watching others suffer. Sympathy for the condemned could turn them against the government: “We secretly condemn the law which inflicts the punishment – <a href="https://collections.nlm.nih.gov/bookviewer?PID=nlm:nlmuid-2569014R-bk">hence arises a want of respect for laws in general</a>,” he wrote in a pamphlet titled “An Enquiry into the Effects of Public Punishments upon Criminals and upon Society.”</p>

<p>Alternatively, repeated exposure to cruelty could harden spectators, encouraging the very violence that punishment was supposed to deter. “How often,” Rush asked, “do we find pockets picked under a gallows, and <a href="https://collections.nlm.nih.gov/bookviewer?PID=nlm:nlmuid-2569014R-bk">highway-robberies committed within sight of a gibbet</a>?” </p>

<p>The crowd could pity the condemned, admire his composure or simply enjoy an outing. Gathering witnesses did not guarantee that they absorbed the intended lesson. The complaint about festive music at Young’s execution exposed that uncertainty: Officials could stage the spectacle, but they could not control its meaning.</p>

<h2>What harm does this prevent?</h2>

<p>Young’s execution gives the proposed broadcast of Hasan’s death a particular resonance. The crimes, jurisdictions and audiences differ, yet the ambition remains recognizable: to make one person’s punishment teach everyone else a lesson – and demonstrate the government’s strength.</p>

<p>Cruelty concerns more than the pain inflicted. It also lies in <a href="https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/17438721241313176">treating a person as fodder for exposure</a>, humiliation and public instruction. The condemned person’s body becomes a public demonstration of whom the state protects – and whom it has the power to destroy.</p>

<p>But spectators may come for the theater of death itself, drawn by fascination with what human beings can do to one another. What officials present as instruction can become the marketing of guilty pleasures.</p>

<p>Cesare Beccaria, <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cesare-Beccaria">an Italian criminologist and economist</a> whose 1764 essay “<a href="https://oll.libertyfund.org/titles/voltaire-an-essay-on-crimes-and-punishments">On Crimes and Punishments</a>” helped shape American reform debates, argued that punishment could not undo a crime, only prevent future harm. Suffering beyond that purpose was unnecessary cruelty.</p>

<p>For Beccaria, an execution’s fleeting spectacle deterred less effectively than lifelong penal servitude. Beccaria’s alternative was harsh, but his principle constrained the state: The power to inflict suffering did not establish its necessity.</p>

<p>At Young’s scaffold, the state could end his life without controlling the meaning of his death. A broadcast would vastly enlarge the audience, but reach is no proof of usefulness, and curiosity supplies no justification.</p>

<p>Beccaria’s question thus remains: What future harm does this additional spectacle prevent? If it prevents none, what justifies it – and what does it reveal about the government that stages it?</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294211/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Religious preschools want public funding, but exemptions from nondiscrimination rules – the Supreme Court will decide if that’s constitutional</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765079/original/file-20261008-50-r44wmo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Religious schools may participate in Colorado&#39;s Universal Preschool Program if they follow its requirements, including antidiscrimination rules. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/childrens-religious-program-royalty-free-image/175408075?phrase=christian%20preschool&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">FatCamera/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>When Colorado launched its <a href="https://cdec.colorado.gov/universal-preschool-colorado">Universal Preschool Program</a> in 2023, the goal was simple: Give every 4-year-old in the state access to free, publicly funded education. To deliver on that promise, the state allowed both public and private providers – including faith-based preschools – to participate, provided they abide by the program’s rules.</p>

<p>Those include a requirement not to discriminate against students or families based on sexual orientation or gender identity – which quickly triggered a legal battle.</p>

<p>Catholic preschool providers and the parents of a preschool-age child <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca10/24-1267/24-1267-2025-09-30.html">challenged the requirement in court</a>, arguing that forcing them to sign the agreement unconstitutionally burdened their faith. They allege that because their religious beliefs teach that marriage is strictly between a man and a woman, complying with state antidiscrimination rules would force them to compromise their religious values.</p>

<p><a href="https://elpa.education.wisc.edu/fac-staff/eckes-suzanne/">As professors</a> <a href="https://education.uconn.edu/person/preston-green-iii/">of education law</a>, we see this case as the latest chapter in a struggle over <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-colorado-preschool-case-will-be-the-supreme-courts-latest-to-test-boundaries-of-lgbtq-rights-and-religious-freedom-290122">how to balance civil rights protections</a> with the rights of religious organizations. <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2026/25-581">St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy</a> is also part of a broader constitutional debate over when and under what conditions <a href="https://theconversation.com/are-religious-charter-schools-constitutional-after-deadlocked-scotus-decision-another-oklahoma-case-is-trying-to-find-out-292892">religious schools may receive public support</a>.</p>

<p>The U.S. Supreme Court will <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/cases/st-mary-catholic-parish-v-roy/">hear oral arguments on Nov. 3, 2026</a>. Justices will be poised to decide a fundamental constitutional question: When state governments extend taxpayer dollars to private institutions, particularly religious ones, can they require those institutions to follow basic antidiscrimination rules?</p>

<h2>Lower courts</h2>

<p>The lower courts largely sided with Colorado. Both a federal district court and the <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca10/24-1267/24-1267-2025-09-30.html">10th Circuit Court of Appeals</a> ruled that the state was not targeting or punishing Catholic preschools because of their faith. </p>

<p>Instead, the courts concluded that Colorado had set a neutral, generally applicable rule for everyone receiving public funds: If you take taxpayer dollars to run a preschool, you cannot turn families away based on who they are. Specifically, the state required participating schools to not exclude LGBTQ+ students, families or staff because of their sexual orientation or gender identity.</p>

<p>The Catholic preschools’ argument had relied heavily on a series of Supreme Court decisions, starting in 2017, that involved religious schools and public funding – and shifted the wall between church and state in education. In <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/582/15-577/">Trinity Lutheran v. Comer</a>, <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/591/18-1195/">Espinoza v. Montana</a> and <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/596/20-1088/">Carson v. Makin</a>, the court ruled that states cannot flatly disqualify religious schools from public grants or tuition assistance programs simply because of their religious character or religious instruction.</p>

<p>The 10th Circuit, however, carefully distinguished Colorado’s program from the ones in those landmark rulings. Colorado does not bar religious schools from participating; faith-based providers are welcome to apply for funding if they follow the same rules that apply to other participating preschools.</p>

<h2>Neutral rule or unconstitutional burden?</h2>

<p>The St. Mary case places two foundational principles of religious freedom law directly at odds.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765081/original/file-20261008-60-nwdchq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large white building with tall pillars stands against a bright blue sky and tall green grass." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765081/original/file-20261008-60-nwdchq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765081/original/file-20261008-60-nwdchq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765081/original/file-20261008-60-nwdchq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765081/original/file-20261008-60-nwdchq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765081/original/file-20261008-60-nwdchq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765081/original/file-20261008-60-nwdchq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765081/original/file-20261008-60-nwdchq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/SupremeCourt/287be2e2f02c43459ae40de4c4c779f5/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=supreme%20court&amp;currentItemNo=23&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib</a></span>

<p><a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-1/">The First Amendment</a> contains two religion clauses. One forbids the government from making laws that establish religion; the other forbids laws that prohibit its “free exercise.”</p>

<p>Since the 1990 decision in <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/494/872/">Employment Division v. Smith</a>, the Supreme Court has followed a straightforward rule: Neutral laws that apply to everyone do not violate the free exercise clause just because they conflict with someone’s religious beliefs. Under this view, Colorado’s nondiscrimination rule is constitutional because it applies to secular and religious preschools alike. </p>

<p>Over the past decade, however, the court’s conservative majority has expanded protections for religious institutions. Rulings like <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2020/19-123">Fulton v. City of Philadelphia</a> have held that neutral rules lose their neutrality if the government creates exceptions based on secular interest while denying them for religious reasons.</p>

<p>In the St. Mary case, the core legal argument hinges on this precise issue. Colorado’s program allows some exemptions to its requirements; for example, preschools in churches may give admissions preference to members of their congregation. The Catholic preschools argue that if the state can make those kinds of exceptions, it is discriminatory not to accommodate exemptions based on religious beliefs.</p>

<p>The Supreme Court must decide whether Colorado’s requirement that participating preschools comply with nondiscrimination rules is simply a neutral condition on receiving state funding, or an unconstitutional burden on religious exercise.</p>

<h2>Stakes far beyond preschool</h2>

<p>While St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy focuses specifically on sexual orientation and gender identity in preschool admissions, the Supreme Court’s ruling will likely have far-reaching consequences for all public funding.</p>

<p>For example, if the court rules that religious organizations have a constitutional right to opt out of state antidiscrimination rules while receiving public funds, that principle may not stop at LGBTQ+ rights.</p>

<p>The Supreme Court addressed one such conflict in a case decided in 1983, <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/461/574/">Bob Jones University v. U.S.</a>. The case combined challenges from two fundamentalist Christian schools that lost their tax-exempt status because of racially discriminatory admissions policies. The schools argued that their discrimination was rooted in their faith, and so they should receive an exemption, but the court rejected their petition 8-1.</p>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/BobJonesUniversity/0a561503042c44058971f878e2cbeae4/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=%22bob%20jones%20university%22&amp;currentItemNo=42&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As today’s Supreme Court has expanded eligibility for religious schools and their students to receive taxpayer money, some legal scholars have questioned whether religious exemptions could eventually <a href="https://nepc.colorado.edu/sites/default/files/publications/PB%20Mead-Eckes%20Privatization_4.pdf">challenge prohibitions against sex</a> and, once again, <a href="https://scholarship.miami.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/The-Potential-for-Race-Discrimination-in/991032088949102976">race discrimination</a>. More broadly, expanding religious-liberty projections may increasingly come into tension with governmental efforts to enforce civil rights protections. </p>

<h2>Public vs. private</h2>

<p>These questions are especially significant in the <a href="https://www.au.org/wp-content/uploads/securepdfs/2026/09/Ben-Gamla-v.-Shellem-District-Court-Order-9.24.26.pdf">emerging litigation</a> over <a href="https://theconversation.com/are-religious-charter-schools-constitutional-after-deadlocked-scotus-decision-another-oklahoma-case-is-trying-to-find-out-292892">whether charter schools can be religious</a>. Charter schools are funded by taxpayers and authorized by states, but courts remain divided over whether they should be <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-a-charter-school-really-supreme-court-ruling-on-whether-catholic-charter-is-constitutional-will-hinge-on-whether-theyre-public-or-private-249428">treated as public schools or private organizations</a>. </p>

<p>Critics argue that religious charter schools would violate the establishment clause because charter schools are public in all but name. Supporters counter that charter operators are private, and that excluding faith-based schools from charter programs violates the free exercise clause. That debate was <a href="https://www.news9.com/oklahoma-city-education/judge-blocks-oklahoma-ben-gamla-charter-school">reignited in September 2026</a>, when a federal judge ruled that Oklahoma could not reject a Jewish organization’s charter proposal solely based on its religious status.</p>

<p>If the Supreme Court rules in favor of St. Mary, and courts ultimately decide that religious charter schools are constitutional, religious operators could argue that states cannot condition public funding on compliance with nondiscrimination requirements that conflict with their faith.</p>

<p>A decision in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy is expected by late spring 2027, and it will likely echo for years to come. Whatever the justices decide, we believe the St. Mary case will shape how states design publicly funded programs that rely on private religious providers, from universal pre-K and foster care agencies to homeless shelters. In the end, the ruling could also determine how far those providers can go in rejecting nondiscrimination rules.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/281965/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Religious schools may participate in Colorado's Universal Preschool Program if they follow its requirements, including antidiscrimination rules
FatCamera/E+ via Getty Images When Colorado launched its Universal Preschool Program in 2023, the goal was simple: Give every 4-year-old in the state access to free, publicly funded education
To deliver on that promise, the state allowed both public and private providers – including faith-based preschools – to participate, provided they abide by the program’s rules
Those include a requirement not to discriminate against students or families based on sexual orientation or gender identity – which quickly triggered a legal battle
Catholic preschool providers and the parents of a preschool-age child challenged the requirement in court , arguing that forcing them to sign the agreement unconstitutionally burdened their faith

They allege that because their religious beliefs teach that marriage is strictly between a man and a woman, complying with state antidiscrimination rules would force them to compromise their religious values
As professors of education law , we see this case as the latest chapter in a struggle over how to balance civil rights protections with the rights of religious organizations
Roy is also part of a broader constitutional debate over when and under what conditions religious schools may receive public support
Supreme Court will hear oral arguments on Nov. 3, 2026

Justices will be poised to decide a fundamental constitutional question: When state governments extend taxpayer dollars to private institutions, particularly religious ones, can they require those institutions to follow basic antidiscrimination rules? Lower courts The lower courts largely sided with Colorado
Both a federal district court and the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the state was not targeting or punishing Catholic preschools because of their faith

Instead, the courts concluded that Colorado had set a neutral, generally applicable rule for everyone receiving public funds: If you take taxpayer dollars to run a preschool, you cannot turn families away based on who they are
Specifically, the state required participating schools to not exclude LGBTQ+ students, families or staff because of their sexual orientation or gender identity

The Catholic preschools’ argument had relied heavily on a series of Supreme Court decisions, starting in 2017, that involved religious schools and public funding – and shifted the wall between church and state in education
Makin , the court ruled that states cannot flatly disqualify religious schools from public grants or tuition assistance programs simply because of their religious character or religious instruction
The 10th Circuit, however, carefully distinguished Colorado’s program from the ones in those landmark rulings
Colorado does not bar religious schools from participating; faith-based providers are welcome to apply for funding if they follow the same rules that apply to other participating preschools
Neutral rule or unconstitutional burden? The St
Mary case places two foundational principles of religious freedom law directly at odds
The Supreme Court will hear arguments in the St
AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib The First Amendment contains two religion clauses
One forbids the government from making laws that establish religion; the other forbids laws that prohibit its “free exercise.” Since the 1990 decision in Employment Division v
Smith , the Supreme Court has followed a straightforward rule: Neutral laws that apply to everyone do not violate the free exercise clause just because they conflict with someone’s religious beliefs
Under this view, Colorado’s nondiscrimination rule is constitutional because it applies to secular and religious preschools alike
Over the past decade, however, the court’s conservative majority has expanded protections for religious institutions
City of Philadelphia have held that neutral rules lose their neutrality if the government creates exceptions based on secular interest while denying them for religious reasons
Mary case, the core legal argument hinges on this precise issue
Colorado’s program allows some exemptions to its requirements; for example, preschools in churches may give admissions preference to members of their congregation
The Catholic preschools argue that if the state can make those kinds of exceptions, it is discriminatory not to accommodate exemptions based on religious beliefs

The Supreme Court must decide whether Colorado’s requirement that participating preschools comply with nondiscrimination rules is simply a neutral condition on receiving state funding, or an unconstitutional burden on religious exercise
Roy focuses specifically on sexual orientation and gender identity in preschool admissions, the Supreme Court’s ruling will likely have far-reaching consequences for all public funding

For example, if the court rules that religious organizations have a constitutional right to opt out of state antidiscrimination rules while receiving public funds, that principle may not stop at LGBTQ+ rights
The Supreme Court addressed one such conflict in a case decided in 1983, Bob Jones University v
The case combined challenges from two fundamentalist Christian schools that lost their tax-exempt status because of racially discriminatory admissions policies
The schools argued that their discrimination was rooted in their faith, and so they should receive an exemption, but the court rejected their petition 8-1
