title: Trump is taking his midterms anger out on Ukraine
excerpt: Donald Trump walks to the White House from the South Lawn on October 10, 2026. | Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff ,
body: Donald Trump walks to the White House from the South Lawn on October 10, 2026. | Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Is Trump turning on Ukraine?  What’s happening? Ukraine says its access to Starlink, the satellite internet system run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company, and Starshield, the military version of the same technology, is being throttled as President Donald Trump’s animosity toward the country mounts

Why is Trump angry with Ukraine? Trump has been hot and cold on Ukraine since he returned to office, but his current anger is driven by oil prices and successful Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries — particularly ahead of the US midterm elections.  Last week, Trump announced a US-Russia diesel deal, which has elicited bipartisan anger and probably won’t do much , if anything, for diesel prices in the US
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticized the deal, leading Trump to lash out and call for Zelenskyy’s replacement

Over the weekend, Trump also announced an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE” between Ukraine and Russia that doesn’t really seem to exist . “Both parties have agreed,” he wrote. “Do not break it!” (Russia appears to have broken it the same day , while Ukraine is complying for now.) Is Ukraine actually to blame for high oil prices? Partially, but not primarily; as the BBC explains , while Ukrainian refinery strikes play a role, ongoing disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf oil industry from Trump’s war with Iran have had a greater impact (though Trump has tried to shift the blame to Ukraine)
Why is Starlink so important? Starlink and Starshield provide vital communications infrastructure in Ukraine, especially on the battlefield
The technology is also used to control offensive and defensive Ukrainian drones, which have emerged as a key part of Ukraine’s military efforts against Russia

What’s next? Despite the fact that neither Russia nor Ukraine seemingly signed on to Trump’s “ENERGY CEASEFIRE” and Russia is still attacking Ukrainian energy facilities , Trump is trying to bind Ukraine to it: The US has reportedly threatened to suspend US intelligence sharing, which has helped give Ukraine early warning of Russian missile attacks, if Ukraine strikes more Russian refineries

And with that, it’s time to log off… I appreciated this New York Times story , pegged to Pope Leo XIV’s diagnosis yesterday, about all of the ways that science has made lung cancer massively more survivable than in years past, with a fatality rate half of what it was in the 1990s
Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: Your flu shot can’t wait
excerpt: Some parts of the country are seeing levels of flu activity typically associated with late fall or early winter. | Deb Cohn-Orbach/UCG/Universal Images Group vi
body: Some parts of the country are seeing levels of flu activity typically associated with late fall or early winter. | Deb Cohn-Orbach/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Flu season is starting earlier than usual this year, which I know from reviewing federal data
But I also know it because I woke up with body aches and chills last night, mere days before I’d planned to get my flu vaccination (!)
Already, some parts of the country are seeing levels of flu activity typically associated with late fall or early winter
In Washington state, for instance, doctors are reporting seeing as much flu now as they usually would around Christmas.  Flu activity overall is still low , to be clear
But as of October 7, infections were rising in all 50 states
And flu is spreading before many people — like, say, me — have received their annual vaccine
Epidemiologists don’t yet know why the flu arrived early this year, or why cases first started rising in Western states like Washington, California, and Nevada
It’s possible that a mutation is helping this year’s flu variants evade existing immunity, one virologist told NPR
International travel could play a role , too: Flu cases also spiked early in Japan and other parts of Asia
We don’t need to know why the flu arrived early to take some basic precautions, though
So today, we’re talking through some practical tips for coping with an early flu season
Go a little deeper View Link An early flu season doesn’t necessarily mean a worse season — but even a moderate season can do serious damage
Last year, influenza sent hundreds of thousands of people to the hospital and caused tens of thousands of deaths, including almost 200 among children
The first and best way to avoid those kinds of harms is by getting the flu shot, which  reduces the risk of serious illness by an average of 40 to 60 percent

In the US, people aged 6 months and older are typically told to get the vaccine by October’s end.  In light of the early onset, however (it takes two weeks to build up full immunity), you might instead want to get your shot ASAP
There are some everyday precautions you can take, too — many of them familiar from the Covid-19 era
Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and warm water, for slightly longer than feels appropriate

Mask when you’re sick or might encounter someone else who is.  And  don’t neglect the good habits that support your overall health: getting enough sleep, drinking a lot of water, and eating a balanced diet. (There’s very little evidence for trendier interventions, like supplements, saunas, cold plunges, or the infused herbal baths that my kooky former yoga teacher used to recommend.)  If you do get flu symptoms, reach out to your doctor early —  especially if you’re older, pregnant, immunocompromised, or otherwise at higher risk for complications
Prescription antiviral medications, like Tamiflu, prevent the flu virus from spreading inside your body so that your immune system can clear it

But they work best within 48 hours of symptom onset.  To be clear, you needn’t take my word on any of this; I’m just another voice in the public health cacophony! Besides, recent polling suggests that my particular voice — that is, the voice of someone who works in media — is not quite as persuasive as it used to be. (Ditto medical websites and government health agencies.) But if you have doubts or questions about vaccines,  there is someone much closer to home you can consult : Ask your doctor (or nurse or pharmacist) about the flu shot’s risks and benefits
They’re best positioned to break the science down and apply it to your health
In hindsight, mine surely would have told me to stop delaying my shot for a more convenient weekend
One link for later ➨ Get creative in the fight against inflation
The latest inflation numbers are out today, and they are pretty bad
The cost of many goods and services is rising more quickly than both consumers’ incomes and economists’ expectations

For me, this news brought to mind a question that Vox’s former personal finance columnist tackled a few years ago: Namely, am I cursed to keep spending more money on more things forever?! Her answer was essentially “yes,” but she offered a few ways to help offset those costs: things like moving to a cheaper area or pooling resources via initiatives like tool libraries and community gardens.  Before you go… Did you know… that Colombia is home to almost 20 percent of all the avian species on Earth? That’s the most of any country, at nearly 2,000 birds
Today’s trivia: Which percussion instrument is famously played by Mississippi State University fans at home football games? (You can find this and other brain puzzles  in Vox’s daily crossword

Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: We asked you for the name of the 2025 Pixar film set in the “Communiverse.” That would be Elio , a movie you may well never have heard of: It  had the worst opening weekend of any Pixar film, ever.

title: The problem with the US surrogacy system
excerpt: For some couples, surrogacy is a miracle: an opportunity to have a child even if they’re unable to conceive one naturally
body: For some couples, surrogacy is a miracle: an opportunity to have a child even if they’re unable to conceive one naturally
Not only is surrogacy expensive — think six figures — but it’s also largely unregulated

And that last part is becoming a bigger problem.  Just last week, a California couple was arrested on child abuse charges after it was revealed that they had over 20 children from different surrogate mothers living in a large mansion in Arcadia, a city near Los Angeles
Many of the surrogates are currently fighting for custody through the courts of the children they carried
The Arcadia case, however, is only the most recent example of how surrogacy can go wrong

Every case is different, but every one illuminates how opaque — and often ripe for abuse or legal issues — the American surrogacy industry is.  Emi Nietfeld is a reporter at Washington Sun who writes about surrogacy, IVF, and how we build families

She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about what’s kept lawmakers from regulating the surrogacy industry, the recent high-profile cases bringing these problems to light, and why more regulation doesn’t necessarily offer a straightforward fix
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity

There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .  The United States does not regulate the surrogacy industry seemingly at all
What is going on? Why not? The lack of federal regulation is both political and financial
Politically, this goes all the way back to the start of IVF

Anti-abortion Republicans were not comfortable with the idea of creating and destroying embryos during IVF, and so they fought against efforts to regulate it.  People on the left were worried that limiting what kinds of technology you could access would lead to the government controlling who could have families
People who think that IVF is murder don’t want to have any surrogacy
And people on the left don’t want the government saying who can and cannot have a family
One of the issues raised by the New Yorker story is that there are surrogacy agencies that connect parents and potential surrogates
And it makes you wonder who gets to do that? Who can own and operate a surrogacy agency in the US today? Anyone
Only one state, New York, requires a special license
And everywhere else it’s easier to open an agency than a hot dog stand or a nail salon
This has resulted in the rise of so-called pop-up agencies where businesses come onto the scene, and nobody really knows who owns them or who’s running them
That has led to many people who aren’t experienced, who sign up with these agencies, then feeling like they weren’t prepared or that they were deceived in entering the agreement
Have we ever tried in the past to regulate this better? Have there been efforts made? In the 1980s, there was the case of Baby M
That was called traditional surrogacy where Mary Beth Whitehead was the surrogate, but it was also her egg
So the child she delivered was genetically related to her
After she gave birth, she changed her mind

She kidnapped the child, went on the run for several months, and it was a national crisis where this was all over the news.  Ultimately, a judge in New Jersey ruled that the surrogacy arrangement was unenforceable
Commercial surrogacy arrangements became illegal in New Jersey, and they stayed illegal in New York until 2020

Part of why regulation looks the way it does is because in 1995, Congress passed a piece of legislation saying that there would be no federal funding for embryo research, which means no federal funding for IVF
That left all of the research, development, innovation up to the free market
And so while that could be seen as an attempt to regulate IVF, it actually meant that those things would no longer be under the government’s purview
In the US, we’ve seen over the past few years some really high-profile cases that are making lawmakers reckon with the fact that we do not have laws around this
There’s the Mark surrogacy case in California, which is both a really unique case and also illustrates some of the fears around Chinese intended parents coming to the United States to have their kids
This is part of larger geopolitical tensions between the US and China, which are playing out in the surrogacy industry
There’s the case of Xu Bo, the Chinese video gaming billionaire who is rumored to have more than 100 children via surrogacy in America

His story taps into fears of birth tourism and people from other countries, especially China, coming to the United States to do surrogacy so that their kids are American citizens.  Republican lawmakers are talking a lot about the idea that people could come from enemy countries, have American citizens, and raise them with the intent that they might one day become spies or president of the United States and be double actors
In Texas, there’s the case of McKenna West, where she learned at 20 weeks’ gestation that the baby was very sick
The intended parents asked her to get an abortion
McKenna went to Texas and began fighting for custody to keep the baby while the parents objected
They wanted the baby, and she petitioned the Supreme Court, which declined to hear the case
And finally, there’s the case of Kyla Simpson in Florida, whom I wrote about for New York Magazine , and she gave birth for a single dad in China who wasn’t there for the birth
He hadn’t applied for a visa to come to the United States, and when he did apply, he was rejected

title: Trump’s bizarre new transit plan could hurt the families who need it most
excerpt: The Trump administration’s transit policies won’t “make travel family-friendly again” in the ways that matter most. | GraphicaArtis/Getty Images “We should look
body: The Trump administration’s transit policies won’t “make travel family-friendly again” in the ways that matter most. | GraphicaArtis/Getty Images “We should look for love!” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy bellowed while flanked by his nine children at the Great American State Fair in June: “Get married, and have lots of kids!” In a brazen attempt to make Duffy’s ethos a matter of policy, the Trump administration announced a strange new plan earlier this month tying a huge tranche of federal funding for public transit to high fertility and marriage rates

If the plan goes into effect, then communities with a high number of traditional nuclear families could get a 10 percent funding boost to build new trains, bus routes, and ferry lines. “If you want federal funding,” Duffy’s Transportation Department said in a statement , then “your project needs to align with where communities and families are actually growing.” Trump, who has dubbed himself the “ fertilization president ,” and his bevvy of neopatriarchal trad – pilled deputies have long nursed a fixation with the country’s declining birth rate
But dubious as this new policy may be, it stumbles upon a genuine pain point in the nation’s public transit systems: They are not nearly as family friendly as they should be

And regardless of whether these discomfitingly pronatalist guidelines ever go into effect as written — and they probably will — they raise important questions about how American families use our transit systems now, and the policies could actually make their lives easier in the long run
The same woes that affect all riders — long wait times, inaccessible stations, inadequate reach, and crowded rush hours — often doubly affect families

That’s one reason why so many of them have fled the nation’s densest, most transit-oriented cities in search of suburbs where they need not lug a stroller up yet another broken escalator to reach a subway platform

Families who can’t afford to trade in their MetroCards and bus passes for minivans may find themselves priced into housing served by especially substandard transit options, funneling them into brutal, hours-long commutes

According to one landmark study, the single strongest factor in predicting social mobility in the US is neither crime nor test scores nor the presence of “traditional” two-parent households, but access to adequate transportation
With every extra minute a child spends commuting to school, they become less likely to move out poverty as an adult
And for that reason alone, American families with kids do deserve special attention when it comes to how and where and why we build public transit

On this, the Trump administration got something right, even if they got there for all the wrong reasons — ones that I, a childless woman of childbearing age, find vaguely ethnonationalist, and above all, personally creepy
But families often need public transportation most in the places where it’s otherwise hardest to raise kids — which is to say in dense cities rather than in already car-centric suburbs
In that sense, especially, In fact, it might make circumstances even worse for the families that really rely on public transit every day

What family-friendly public transit actually looks like Marriage and birth rates might sound like a reasonable proxy for where families live, but in reality, according to an analysis by the Urban Institute, the places with the most “ traditional” nuclear families tend to be whiter and wealthier than the population at large, and are much more likely to get around by car, not trains or buses

We are talking about the suburbs here, which, while certainly deserving of their own transit infrastructure, rarely rely on trains or buses the way that a carless family living on the outer edges of a major city might
And yet the Trump administration has typically treated those very communities — some of which do, in fact, have high birth rates — with contempt or even outright antipathy
Consider Chicago’s Red Line, the busiest corridor of the city’s L rail system, which serves some 138 million people per year
The line has long been in need of expansion, and a $5.7 billion extension close to 60 years in the making finally broke ground earlier this year
It will add 5.5 more miles of track with four new stations in the city’s southernmost neighborhoods

For over half a century, families in the far South Side of Chicago have cobbled together grueling commutes that force them to transfer from buses and trains to reach downtown Chicago, which helps explain why unemployment and poverty rates in the area remain so stubbornly high

Communities like Roseland, where many of the new stations will be built, are considered to be among the most challenging places in the nation to raise a child , but thousands of local families still find ways to do so
Roseland has a much higher birth rate than the national average, meaning that in theory, Duffy’s transportation department should be itching to send extra funds to transit projects there
But first they have to be willing to fund it at all, and if past policies hold, they may be reluctant to do just that

Just last year, the Trump administration opted to freeze federal funds already allocated to the Red Line extension , plunging the long-awaited project into yet another prolonged period of infrastructural purgatory

That move plays into a broader pattern: The Trump administration has hampered dozens of transit projects like the Red Line, seemingly in its broader push to starve Democratic-led cities of federal infrastructure dollars

While a federal judge eventually intervened to allow the Red Line extension to proceed , if the Trump administration’s new guidelines go into effect after public comments close in November, then more projects like it in other urban communities will likely be deprioritized
Ultimately, it is the suburbanites who are most poised to benefit from the Trump administration’s proposed policy

An example is FrontRunner 2X in Utah, a commuter rail project that will slash travel time for Utahns traveling across the state, and will also help Salt Lake City shoulder an influx of tourists when it hosts the Olympics in 2034
It received federal support through the same tranche of funding as Chicago’s Red Line extension
In stark contrast with that more urban initiative, FrontRunner 2X has been the rare public transit project to receive continued support under the Trump administration

Utah has some of the highest birth and marriage rates in the country, so it’s not a stretch of the imagination to say that if the Trump administration has its way, then the United States will see more projects like FrontRunner 2X get funded, while others like the Red Line extension face bureaucratic bottlenecks and funding freezes

Roseland’s high birth rate notwithstanding, the neighborhood has some of the lowest marriage rates in the country, meaning that even if a project there did manage to eke out federal support, then according to this new calculus, it would still receive significantly less funding from the federal government than a place like the suburbs of Salt Lake City where married families with children are more common

Trump’s new pronatalist transit agenda is, at the very least, an indication that after two years spent twiddling their thumbs, firing Amtrak executives , and venerating cars big and small , he may finally be building a semi-coherent transit strategy

And his Transportation Department has allowed a few genuinely family-friendly upgrades for the country’s transit infrastructure to proceed, including grants to add space for strollers on trains and buses
But you can’t claim to support American families while siphoning federal dollars away from the projects that could actually be transformational to their lives

I am not one to decry a commuter rail renaissance, but it shouldn’t come at the expense of places where American families — the ones Duffy says he’s so keen on having more babies — don’t have any other choice but to wait an hour for the bus to get to work.

title: Universal childcare is set to be a 2028 presidential test
excerpt: Ro Khanna of California introduced the Free Child Care for America Act, an $80 billion-a-year proposal to make childcare free for nearly every family with kids
body: Ro Khanna of California introduced the Free Child Care for America Act, an $80 billion-a-year proposal to make childcare free for nearly every family with kids under six

The bill would let families choose between sending their child to a daycare center, having a relative, friend, or neighbor paid a living wage to care for them, or taking a $1,000 monthly stipend to keep the child home for the first three years

It comes from a lawmaker who openly says he’s considering a run for president. “I want 2028 to be a big-ideas primary,” Khanna told ABC . “A contest on who’s going to have ideas of the future that meet the moment.” Khanna’s is not the only big Democratic childcare proposal released in the last few months

In July, Project 2029 — a group of liberal policy experts developing an agenda for the next Democratic administration — proposed something similar to Khanna’s plan: giving families a choice between free daycare and $1,000 a month to provide care at home or pay a trusted caregiver
The group estimates that would cost about $200 billion annually

Third Way, a centrist Democratic think tank, unveiled its own universal childcare pitch , guaranteeing every family at least three affordable options within a 15-minute drive of home or work by expanding home-based, infant, and after-hours care, and leveraging employers as partners.  Key takeaways Childcare is emerging as a major 2028 issue, with big new proposals from Rep
Ro Khanna, Project 2029, and Third Way. “Universal childcare” means different things to different people — free for all, affordable for most, or simply enough slots to go around
Polls show broad, bipartisan appetite for government action on childcare, with debate over how much families should chip in
Early childhood policy is quickly becoming a defining issue for 2028 hopefuls
On the right, Vice President JD Vance has staked out an early and controversial position, to pay married stay-at-home parents roughly $9,000 per child annually using existing federal childcare funds
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is spearheading a new House working group to develop a federal childcare plan
Andy Beshear has been pushing free pre-K for all 4-year-olds , something California Gov
Gavin Newsom has already enacted in his state

And New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who can’t run for president but is widely seen as an influential voice in the party’s future, has made universal childcare one of the top goals of his administration
Michelle Lujan Grisham, the Democratic governor of New Mexico, recently told Semafor that any politician seeking to run for president in 2028 “absolutely should” run on universal childcare proposals
Last year New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to families regardless of income
Her advice echoed David Plouffe, a Democratic strategist who managed Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign, who said that universal childcare should be in the Democrats’ 2028 party platform
This new wave of enthusiasm marks a pivot for an idea that has long been seen as a distant pipe dream in American politics
It wasn’t always that way: When women filled factories during World War II, the federal government funded thousands of daycare centers to watch their kids
In 1971, Congress actually passed a bipartisan childcare bill, though President Richard Nixon vetoed it , saying it would weaken the family
In the 50 years since, Washington lawmakers have focused their energies on other big battles, offering little on childcare beyond subsidies for some low-income families
Over that time, the US has fallen out of step with nearly all its peer nations around the world, which help parents pay for childcare, on top of offering paid parental leave after birth
It’s not hard to understand why the idea is finally getting a serious look in the US
With voters citing affordability as a top concern, politicians are looking for ways they can bring down costs facing families
After paying rent or a mortgage, childcare often stands as many parents’ biggest monthly expense
Businesses have started to care too, as access to reliable care affects both people’s ability to hold down jobs and businesses’ ability to attract and retain workers
It’s why organizations like the Chamber of Commerce have taken up the issue and why red, blue, and purple states alike have been elevating childcare in recent years

In Congress and in the Democratic campaign world, there’s a strong sense that childcare, long overshadowed by climate, infrastructure, voting rights, and health care, is now at the front of the line should Democrats regain power
Insiders credit both donor influence and a feeling that childcare advocates have duly waited their turn

But as Democrats begin jockeying for 2028 and universal childcare becomes a rallying cry, it’s also become clear that there’s a big unanswered question at the heart of the politicking: No one yet agrees on what “universal childcare” actually means

Does it refer to care that’s totally free, or just affordable? Is it for everyone, like public school, or targeted at families below an income line? Does it start at birth, and include parents who stay home? Are employers involved, or neighbors and grandparents?  The answers will determine who benefits, how much it costs, and whether the party’s next big promise to families is one it can actually keep
What is universal childcare? When I asked Rep
Khanna how he defines universal childcare, he said that it means “childcare should be free” and that families should have flexibility and choice of how to get that care

Workers, he added, should also be paid a living wage in a universal childcare system.  Later, he described the vision for universal childcare as a public good, akin to public school. “From the time a child is born to the time they’re finished college,” he argued, America has the wealth to provide for kids’ education and development.  Others, however, are defining the idea differently
Linda Smith, who leads Child Care Trust, a national policy think tank, helped design the military’s well-regarded childcare system and oversaw federal early childhood programs under Obama
Earlier this summer, she released a framework for universal childcare that emphasized it does not inherently mean free care

Smith says she wrote it after realizing that even the legislative staffers drafting childcare bills didn’t mean the same thing by the term. “After some candid conversations with congressional staff this summer working on child care policy, it became clear that there are many interpretations of ‘universal child care,’” she wrote on LinkedIn . “If we can’t agree on what the term means, we can’t build durable policy around it.” She argues the “universal childcare” slogan tends to blur three separate goals: universal access , universal affordability , and universal free care
Her vision for universal childcare policy would be a system where all families have access to “affordable, high-quality options” that reflect their needs

Her organization estimates that about 4.2 million children under six with all available parents in the workforce lack a childcare slot within a reasonable distance of home, and she warns that cutting costs without adding new supply could worsen shortages and leave families without available options
Her answer is a mix of building more supply and sharing the cost

title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
excerpt: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next
body: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next
Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk
The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify

Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.  These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach

But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information

Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely
There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly
But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization
Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth
What are the benefits of open models? Let’s start with the basics
A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API
An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available

Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.  Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development
But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one
Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives
They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so
If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research
When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses
But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering
They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications
Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models
Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla
And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure

But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.” Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have

In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like

The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses
If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it

Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience
But open models are not a geopolitical panacea

Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands

He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations

Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models. “I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.” Are open models riskier than closed ones? The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models

There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic , several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude
So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit
Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks
When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts
But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model
There are other important lines of defense
AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no

title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
excerpt: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few y
body: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old
But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money

He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says
The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups

Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged
Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs
SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April
Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents
Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models
Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026
CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales
Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business
Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools

Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”  Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets
Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs
Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls
Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined
Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear
No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives

Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code
That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening

This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records
And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups

Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too
But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans
He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use
There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls
The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees

To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker , this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales
While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations
Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it
Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer
Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first
Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.  Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

title: The rise and fall of a MAGA princess
excerpt: President Donald Trump and US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle in the White House on March 26, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images This sto
body: President Donald Trump and US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle in the White House on March 26, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, is out of a job after serious corruption allegations.  What happened? Guilfoyle resigned on Tuesday after being shown the door earlier in the day by Trump’s brand-new White House press secretary, who announced at a briefing that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign.  Her departure comes just six days after a bombshell Wall Street Journal story , which described Guilfoyle’s efforts to solicit money from a Trump donor, including $100,000 to pay down a credit card bill, in exchange for access to Trump officials and conservative media figures.  Guilfoyle also attempted to conceal those efforts: In one text to the donor, Eric Deters, she wrote, “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing.” Who is Guilfoyle? Fallen MAGA royalty
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality, is also the ex-fiancée of Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. (and, more distantly, the ex-wife of current California Gov
There appears to be little love lost between Guilfoyle and Trump, however
On Tuesday, he told reporters that Guilfoyle “wasn’t a member of my family

She I guess dated my son a long time ago.” (The Don Jr.-Guilfoyle relationship is thought to have ended in 2024.) Why was she forced out? Corruption allegations are not, generally speaking, dealbreakers in Trumpworld; the president and his children are all innovators when it comes to profiting off the presidency , and there’s plenty of self-dealing going on around them
That being said, Guilfoyle may have crossed the line in two specific ways: one, her alleged corruption benefited her and not the Trump family
And two, the allegations are embarrassingly unsubtle even by the standards of the second Trump administration
The combination appears to have been too much

body: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent

title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
excerpt: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace prize has been awarded
body: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”

title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
excerpt: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane
body: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb
It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
As a result of the strong El Niño , it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season

The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered
